Uniform Title: *Śaivāgamādimāhātmya* Author: Jñānaprakāśa Manuscript: IFP/EFEO transcript T00372, pages 1192–1261
Description: Jñānaprakāśa was a renowned Siddhāntin who informs us in the colophon of this text that he resided in Śālīvāṭipura in Tamil Nadu.
He belonged to the fifteenth century and was a prolific writer. There are...

Several of his works are found among the IFP transcripts. In this hymn to the *Śaivāgamamahāśrī*, Jñānaprakāśa praises Śiva as the source of the Āgama, beginning by describing how these scriptures originate as sound (*nāda*) from Him.
He establishes that the authority of the Śaiva scriptures is equal to or even greater than that of the Vedas. Furthermore,
he describes their extent, number, and contents.
Notes: Data entered by the staff of Muktabodha under the supervision of Mark S. G. Dyczkowski. Revision 0: September 18, 2011.
Country of publication: India.
The Greatness of the Śaiva Āgamas and Other Texts, composed by Guru Jñānaprakāśa, a resident of the venerable village of Śālīvāṭi;
pp.
1192–1261 were copied from a manuscript belonging to Śundaradīkṣitar.
Ṭirunelveli Jñānaprakāśa was a renowned Siddhāntin who informs us...
The colophon of this text states that he lived in Śālīvāṭipura in Tamil Nadu.
He belonged to the fifteenth century and was a prolific writer; there are several of his works among the IFP transcripts. In this hymn to the glory...

In the *Jñānaprakāśa*, a work of the *Śaivāgama*, [the author] praises Śiva as the source of the *āgama* and begins by describing how these [scriptures] originate as sound from the core of Sadāśiva’s consciousness. He establishes the authority of...
"The Śaiva scriptures are equal to or even greater than those of the Vedas. He also describes their extent, number, and contents:
"Obeisance to Śiva, to Śakti, to the eternal Bindu, to the Guru, and to Gaṇeśa."
To the wise Kārttikeya:

some, relying on the doctrine of those who deny Īśvara, maintain that the Śiva-āgamas possess authority because they are uncreated (*akṛta*), whereas [they argue] there is no authority for those that are created (*kṛta*).
Even if this [text] possesses some degree of authority in some way, those of weak intellect claim that it concerns "human beings whose names have fallen from the path of the Vedas. That is not so;
for even having assumed the form of the Five-faced One with his five faces, [he spoke thus].
The Lord declared that the entire web of faith beginning with the Vedas has emerged from the supreme cause, Śiva, who is peaceful and whose form is unperceived;
it is established that all scripture has issued forth in the form of *nāda* (the primordial sound).
And from the Pauṣkara-Śivāgama scripture:
"Furthermore, the limbs [of the Veda], the four Vedas, Mīmāṃsā, Nyāya-vistara, Purāṇa,
and Dharmaśāstra— these constitute the fourteen [vidyās]."

Āyurveda, Yajurveda, and Gāndharvaveda follow in sequence; after that, the science of weapons (astra-śāstra)—these are remembered as the eighteen branches of knowledge (vidyās). He is the original author of these eighteen sciences, which proceed along diverse paths.
The Śruti declares that the Poet (Kavi) is indeed Śūlapāṇi himself.
The eighteen Purāṇas have been described in brief;
among them, the Sage (Muni) is the seer during the Dvāpara ages within the various cycles of creation.
Just as Vyāsa, the son of Satyavatī, is Mahādeva himself who revealed the *Kāmika* and other scriptures,
he is the author of the eighteen *Āgamas*, beginning with the *Kāmika*.
Regarding its divisions, as for example: "The Lord Maheśvara [is the author].

Thus, because the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā, Dharmasaṃhitā, Sūta-saṃhitā, and the Śruti texts such as the Kāmika and others were composed by Śiva himself, they possess authority. Furthermore, regarding their validity...

Because [the Vedas] were brought forth through the incarnation of Nārāyaṇa by means of *nyāsa*, and because of the reply in the *Sūta-saṃhitā* stating that even when [the world] was measured, this [Veda] remained as a residue, the authority of both the Vedas and the Śiva-āgamas rests solely upon their being composed by the Supreme Lord, Paraśiva.

It is not by virtue of being uncreated. If it is argued that the Vedas are eternal because they consist of letters, words, and sentences—just like the compositions of Kālidāsa and others—and because they are effects that pre-exist [in their causes], then the Śaiva Āgamas would also be eternal.
For the *Sūtasamhitā-vṛtti* states: "The non-existent does not come into being, nor does the existent cease to exist."
And as for the words: the authority of the Vedas and the Śiva-āgamas rests solely on their being composed by the supremely trustworthy Paraśiva, and not on their being uncreated, because—
like the statements of Kālidāsa and others— they consist of letters, words, sentences, and utterances, and thus exist as effects produced from causes.

Regarding the phrase "the Vedas were made by you by the wise"—likewise, in the commentary on the *Sahasranāma* regarding the term *kṛtāgamāya*, it means: he by whom the *āgamas*—specifically the various tantras such as the *Kāraṇa*, *Kāmika*, and others—were made or composed, is *kṛtāgama*. Thus [it is said].

"Those beginning with the Coktakāmika and ending with the Vātula, spoken by Śiva, are the Śivāgamas"—thus it was explained by Alaṅkāra Dīkṣita. Therefore, precisely because they were composed by Śiva, both [the Vedas and the Āgamas] are authoritative; and this has been stated in the *Caturvedārthataṭparyasaṃgraha*: "The Vedas..."

Even while merely asserting "this is the authority," people understand that the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is the ultimate limit of speech; yet another [sees] the object of meditative discourse as having a form composed of the elements from the peak down to the root, for aeons. This is the authority.
O Great Sage, if these [teachings] have been set forth by the Ṛṣis, why are they not authoritative for us?
It is not possible for you to say that other systems (tantrāntara) are corrupted because they have been accepted [by others].
Regarding the phrase "those which have Śiva as their author," it is stated in the Vāyavīya Saṃhitā:
"That which has been composed by me, whose every defect is unborn [non-existent] and who is omniscient, is the word of Śiva."
That is authoritative, there is no doubt.
Therefore, the words of the Lord are to be trusted by the wise.
Regarding merit and demerit, they correspond to reality; one who lacks faith in them goes to a lower state. Thus it is said.
Just as the Vedas mutually supplement one another, both [the Veda and the Āgama] possess authority through their own independence; as it is stated in the *Mataṅga*:
"The single authoritative means is that statement which is spoken by the Lord and is true."
Thus it is said. In the Pauṣkara as well:
"His word is the sole authority; it is true, a treasure-house of the highest good, and eternal.
Likewise, Śivapūjā has been explained by the venerable Vidyāraṇya in the Sūtasaṃhitā.
"O best of the twice-born, there are two [types of practice], the Vedic and the Tantric; however, that [practice] is Tantric,
belonging only to a Tantrika and not to anyone else, for he is a Vedic practitioner whose root is the Veda."

The Vedic method is that set forth in the Smṛtis, Purāṇas, and so forth; the [Śaiva] method is that set forth in the Kāmika and other Āgamas proclaimed by Śiva, which do not depend upon those [Vedic sources].

In that context, he states the specific qualification for the Tantric practitioner with the words "of the Tantric alone," meaning only for one who has been purified by initiations (*dīkṣā*) and other rites preceded by the construction of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), the mandala, and so forth.
For instance, [the Tantras] do not function independently of one another like the Vedas.

Because it has been stated that the Śiva-āgamas are outside the Veda, yet this Tantra is the essence of the Veda, being both superior to the Veda and a specific part of the Veda; as it is said in the Vāyavya-saṃhitā of the Śaiva Purāṇa-sambhava:
"O Blessed One, we wish to hear the essence of the Vedas, the knowledge of Śiva, as spoken by Śiva himself, for the sake of faith through hearing it. And in the *Makuṭa*:

This is the essence of the Vedas and their core; therefore, one should practice according to the Vedas. This knowledge consists of the meaning of the Vedānta, the supreme and auspicious final conclusion (siddhānta). It is the most excellent, arising from the upward stream (ūrdhvasrotas), comprising twenty-eight tantras, and bestowing the essential meaning of the Vedas.
Regarding the proof that [the Śaiva system] is distinct from the objects of knowledge and other systems:
in the *Suprabheda*, it is said—“The Śaiva, Pāśupata, Soma, and Lākula [systems] are fourfold; among these, the Śaiva...”

The Saiva tradition is remembered as consisting of the twenty-eight tantras beginning with the Kāmika, including those that are peaceful (saumya), fierce (raudra), and such as the Pāśupata; that alone is declared to be the peaceful,
for it is indeed the Siddhānta.
"Other than that, the Raudra Tantra is said to be the Pāśupata and so forth.
And in the Kāmika:
"The Siddhānta is the essence of the Vedas; other [systems] are excluded from the Veda."
In our established doctrine, the conduct prescribed is called Vedic conduct;
and whatever is to be performed as a duty must be practiced provided it is not in conflict with Śaiva ritual action.
If something is contradictory, it should be abandoned; however, one must not abandon the Śaiva [teaching]. Everything that is non-contradictory to the words of Śiva should be accepted as Vedic.
That which is Śaiva is said to be Vedic, and that which is Vedic is indeed Śaiva.
The Śaiva system is both internal and external to the Vedic; that [Vedic] is even lower than the Śaiva.
Nevertheless, the Śaiva is superior to the Vedic, for there is nothing higher than it.
The Siddhānta, consisting of the Kāmika and other scriptures, is unsurpassed; there is nothing more excellent than this.

"O Lord of Sages, although Śaivism is the root and the four Vedas have originated from it, yet because of such statements as 'the Vaidika [system] is the essence of the Vedas,' Śaivism is proclaimed everywhere; for their purpose is one and the same."

Now, is it not the case that one class of Śrauta [scripture] is the essence of the Veda and its mantras are dependent, while another class of Śrauta, such as the Kāmika and others, is the essence of non-Vedic [Tantra] and its Tantra is independent? This has been stated in the Vāyavīya Saṃhitā:

The Śaiva Āgama is also traditionally held to be twofold: Śrauta (based on the Vedas) and Aśrauta (independent). The Śrauta is considered to consist of the essence of the Śrutis, while the other is regarded as independent (svatantra). The independent [Āgama] is first of ten kinds, and then again of eighteen kinds, beginning with the Kāmika.
Established by its own authoritative designations, it is known as the Siddhānta;
it consists of the essence of the Śrutis, has an extent of one hundred crores [of verses], and therein the supreme Pāśupata vow and knowledge are expounded.

(1197) This being the case, it is true that what is stated in the *Makuṭa* and other scriptures—that the *Kāmika* and so forth constitute the essence of the Veda—is indeed correct. Regarding the status of being the essence of the Veda, which supports its scriptural authority, there are two types; of these, the first is as follows:
Within the hundreds of millions of detailed expositions of the Śaiva, Pāśupata, Prati-bhāsa, Tantravaidika, and Pāśupata systems of valid cognition, there exists a certain [text] that, unlike others,
is seen to be independent and in accordance with the Vedas; this constitutes the object of the second Siddhānta.

Furthermore, regarding the detailed exposition of categories and so forth found in independent tantras such as the *Kāmika*, their being the essence of the Veda does not consist in their being produced from the Veda— like butter from curds—
or in their following the Veda, or in their being pervaded by the Veda.

The meaning of "being in accordance with the Vedas" (*vedānusāritva*), even if something else has been said, is "acceptance from the Veda," and not because it pervades the Vedas. As it is stated in the *Vāyavīya Saṃhitā*:
"Whatever is stated in other scriptures that exists in the Śiva-āgamas is not [otherwise] seen."

The certainty of the *Neti-śāstra*—as stated in the *Kāmika* and other Siddhānta scriptures—is that what exists in the knowledge of Śiva is not found elsewhere; thus, there is no higher knowledge than this.
In the *Cintyaviśva*, it is proclaimed that among the other scriptures, the twenty-eight Tantras are known as the Siddhānta.
And the supreme state of Śiva should be known as the sole leader of all principles; it should be known as consisting of all mantras and as being composed of all deities.

"And through austerities in other births, there arises knowledge of the true path. Furthermore, in the *Aruṇācala-māhātmya* it is said: "There is no sacred field superior to Śoṇādri; there is none superior to the five-syllabled Self. There is none...
"There is no dharma other than that of Maheśvara, nor any scripture other than the Śivāgama.
1198) However, because contradiction regarding the object of knowledge (*prameya*) is inherently rooted in contradiction regarding the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), [the two] are mutually...
Just as in the case of the Vedas, by setting aside merely the contradictions in the methods of explaining certain portions of objects of knowledge— such as the doctrine of a single self—
and by avoiding the lack of authoritative injunctions and prohibitions prescribed by the Vedas, there is non-contradiction due to the unity of purpose in many respects; such is the Vedic practice.
By accepting the meaning of the Veda, [one recognizes] those who are experts in the Śaiva-Veda; thus it is stated in the *Suprabheda*:
"Through one's own mantra, one attains the status of being a progenitor of the Veda, characterized by the capacity to reach meanings both already understood and not yet understood within the Veda.
The very nature of the Śiva-āgama as the Śaiva-Veda—being a specific excellence of the Veda—is indeed the essence of the Veda.
The meaning is concluded: it is like the state of being human (*manuṣyatva*), which is a specific quality of the human birth, such as *brāhmaṇatva*. As it is said in the *Mokṣakārikā*:
"Even though it has proceeded toward the contradiction of the fetters and [false] views, it does not abandon its status as a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇatām*)."
Since all those nooses [of worldly activity] belong to him here in every respect,
and their authority is not subverted within their own domain,
the practices of the castes and stages of life are indeed authorized therein.

Nor is its object obstructed by any other means of valid cognition; furthermore, the agency of even Viṣṇu is preceded by the impulsion of the Lord (Paśupati). Thus, both the *Mohaśūrottara* and the *Purāṇas* are sublated by the Vedas, as are the statements found in those [non-Vedic] scriptures. And this is common [to all].
And there is the statement in the *Viśeṣaśaivavaiśiṣṭika*: "These forms of the Supreme Lord [are located] in the Śāla pavilions at Vṛddhācala. Furthermore, in the *Vṛddhācalamāhātmya* it is said:
"These indeed are the forms of the Supreme Lord in the Śāla pavilions at Vṛddhācala."

Having established [the deities] in their respective places, he performed worship according to the specific methods taught in the Śiva-āgamas; furthermore, regarding this matter, there is a manifold distinction here.

Being outside the Veda (*vedabāhyatva*) consists precisely in propounding meanings contrary to the Veda, and not in being so in every respect; for if it were the latter, then all other scriptures such as those of the Cārvākas and others— besides the Śaiva teachings— would also be "outside the Veda," since they too, in some way or another, propound meanings contrary to the Veda.

It would be difficult for the scripture to be [authoritative]. In that regard, although among the various Śiva-āgamas— just as among the various Vedas— there may exist, in some instances, the presentation of meanings contrary to the Vedas,
they do not possess the status of being outside the Veda (vedabāhyatva), just as all other treatises such as those of the Cārvākas and others likewise [do not].
Since they somehow possess the quality of establishing meanings that are not contradictory to the Veda, they are not entirely outside the Veda;
thus, their respective means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are indeed fruitful. As it has been said in the *Śivāgama* and in the *Gurukṛti*:
The Cārvākas are established in the aggregate of the elements (tanmātra);

the Smārtas in the ego (ahaṃkāra); the Vaiśeṣikas in the intellect-principle (buddhitattva), as are the Mānasas and the Indriyas; those who maintain the doctrine of primordial matter (prakṛti) reside in that principle; and the Ārhatas reside in the principle of the qualities (guṇa).
The Pāñcarātrikas abide in Prakṛti; the Vedāntins, Sāṃkhyas, and Yogins abide in Puruṣa; the Śaivas and Paurāṇikas abide in Rāga; and the Somas and Āvidyas abide in Pada.
The Kāpālas are established in the *kalās*; the Kāleśvaras abide in *kāla*;
the Niyatīśas reside within the *kalās*. These are situated separately and have arisen from Him.
(In the *vaśya* [power], those who know the end of the quarters and the Sāṃkhyas and Yogins abide in *puruṣa*.)

The Pāśupatas, however, having established [the soul] within Māyā, observe the Great Vow (mahāvrata). Even those who are agents (*kartṛ*) employed in the region of Pravāheśvara, they remain established in the principle (*tattva*) of Sadāśiva.

Those who speak of the connection with Śiva are the Śaivas; those [who worship] Śakti are the Śāktas. By the wise, they are remembered as being common [to all]. The Siddhāntin stands intent upon the attainment of union (*sāyujya*) with Śiva;
thus, this very state is also described as union with Śiva—not liberation through the annihilation of the self, nor the state of a bound soul (*paśu*).

Liberation here is the realization of the identity of Śiva and the individual soul; it is not the swallowing up of ignorance, nor its destruction, nor the dissolution of the qualities (guṇas), nor even the liberation of a stone. That which is the nature of the Self—manifest upon the departure of the three impurities, consisting of consciousness and bliss—is described as union (sāyujya); it is all-pervading and indeed identical with Śiva.

"Thus ends the Tārye-pavarga. Therefore, it is established—without even needing to state that the Śiva-śāstra is superior to the general Ārṣa-sūtra-śāstra and others precisely because its authorship was performed by Śiva, whose greatness is directly established by the Śruti—that [the former] possesses such excellence. For this reason, O Sūta...

"O best of sages, this [dharma] arising from the *Saṃhitās* and so forth is superior to the dharma arising from the *Srotas*; the dharma arising from the *Ūrdhvasrotas* is superior to the dharma arising from the *Srotas*;
the *Smārta* dharma is greater than the dharma arising from the *Ūrdhvasrotas*;
and the *Śrauta* dharmas are most excellent compared to the *Smārta* ones."
In some instances, even a meaning stated otherwise is sublated by the pure Great Saying (mahāvākya) of Śiva;
for the Śiva-āgama is superior to the Veda, as is heard from its origin from the mouth of Īśāna.
This has been stated in the glorious Hālāsya-mahātmya:
O Brahmins, the divine Śiva-knowledges, beginning with the *Kāmika*,
arise from the upper face of the illustrious Lord Hālāsyanātha;
furthermore, they arise from the face of that same God known as Puruṣa, consisting of twenty-one divisions.
Yukta taught the Ṛgveda; Adhora taught the Yajurveda with its one hundred branches;
Vāma taught the Sāmaveda with its thousand branches; and Sadyojāta taught the Atharvaveda divided into nine parts, O Goddess.
And in the Śrīkāmika:
"From the upper face, that of Īśāna, arises knowledge, which consists of the nature of being an effect and so forth;
and the Ṛg, Yajus, Sāman, and Atharvan Vedas arise from the faces beginning with that of Puruṣa."
In the same way, there are the systems known as Mantra and Tantra, which issued from the mouth of Sadāśiva; namely, Siddhānta,
Gāruḍa, Vāma, Bhūtatantra, and Bhairava,
located respectively in the upper, eastern, northern, western, and [other] directions, beginning with the Cakra and following the sequence.

Therefore, just as in the case of the means of valid cognition such as direct perception, all scriptures— including those composed by the Cārvākas and others, as well as the Śaiva Siddhāntas— whether authored by a single authoritative person, by multiple authorities, or by both, [should be understood] according to their respective forms regarding objects already known or not yet known.

Having gone [to the truth], the validity of the general and the particular, the pervaded and the pervader, the definition and the essential nature, the probandum and the probans, the limited and the unlimited, is established; for indeed,
each individual's own system alone is not the authority, such being the case, [the status of] the Sugata [is proven].

If Kapila were omniscient, then the authority [of the Sāṃkhya system] would not be established; or if both were omniscient, how could there be a difference between them? Since it is impossible to explain this, all scriptures would become invalid, and thus the undesirable consequence of universal confusion would ensue.
Therefore, all scriptures are indeed authoritative within their own respective limits;
this has been established by the venerable Śivācārya Rāmakaṇṭha in the *Vṛttiviveka* on the *Raurava*.

And it is said in the Pauṣkara: "The other path as well— beginning with the Vedas— which reveals the meaning of the bound souls (paśu) and their fetters (pāśa), and which has Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and others as its agents, extends up to the limit of the principles (tattva) taught by [the Lord] himself."

It has been stated that [this path] is not the work of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and others, because the path to liberation is eternal; it bestows the enjoyments of heaven and other realms while one remains [in this world]. Nor is it the word of sages (ārṣa), nor of human beings, nor likewise of divine sages (daivika).

Neither by the gods nor by Brahmā was the word of Viṣṇu obstructed, as it is like a lotus in a forest; likewise, neither by Hari nor by Rudra was the word of Rudra, which is of the nature of Śiva, obstructed.
He who is superior to those who are themselves superior is the one whose authority is supreme and cannot be subverted.
All scripture is established in accordance with the Śiva-āgama, not in accordance with other scriptures, nor by way of agreement with them;
for the Śiva-śāstra is that which establishes [all], since it is the authority for whatever [is to be established]. Of which...
"For whatever extent of universal application is intended for a particular scripture, O Brahmins, its authority shall extend only that far.
This has also been indicated in the *Sūtagītā*:
Established according to the method prescribed in the Tantras, she is worthy of praise by those seeking the ultimate goal,
and she is to be served and worshipped by the followers of the Vedas.
Indeed, the king [should honor] all the Vaidikas as well as the Tantrikas without exception.
One who is most intoxicated with pride should always establish [the community] in a state free from confusion;
he should protect all kings by means of food, drink, clothing, and other necessities.
But surely, it was previously stated that all scriptures, beginning with the Vedas, have Śiva as their author;
now, however, another path is mentioned where the Vedas and so forth have Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and others as their authors.
By saying "Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and others," a great contradiction arises. True, [regarding] the Vedas and so forth...
All scripture and the Śiva-scripture emerge from the mouth of Śiva within Mahāmāyā as the essence of *nāda*;

yet, when manifested again through the composition of phonemes, words, and sentences—whether with or without a formal substratum (*sādhikaraṇa* or *niradhikaraṇa*)—they are the work of Śiva. Thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever. As it is said in the venerable *Kāmika*:

The worldly, the Vedic, and likewise the spiritual, as well as the Transcendent Path (atimārga)—the Tantra known as Mantra is one, yet manifold. The Siddhānta is the Mantra-tantra, while the Atimārga is superior to that; [then there is] the Adhyātma.
That which is lower than that is indeed the Vaidhika;
the Laukika is inferior to the Vaidika. The five deities beginning with Brahmā—Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, Mahāghora, Pūṣan, and Īśāna—are its forms.
Each of them had five faces, and by them the worldly [sciences] and so forth were spoken.
From the *sadyojāta* mantra emerged the one named Brahmā, the seer of all things;
by him indeed was the worldly scripture brought down into the world of mortals.
Grammar, poetics, etymology, prosody,
and indeed astrology, the science of archery, the teachings of Vātsyāyana and others,
the science of longevity, the science of weaponry, and the Ayurveda of trees;
Lokāyata, as well as Sāṃkhya, the doctrine of the Arhat, Mīmāṃsā, Daṇḍanīti, and the worldly sciences such as Vārtā— these are considered non-transcendental (alaukika).
Viṣṇu, the lord of the left-hand mantra, is the second causal lord. By him were indicated the eighteen Purāṇas,
the Dharmaśāstra, the Vedānta, the Pāñcarātra, and the Buddhist [scriptures].
Rudra emerged from the Terrible One (Aghora) and composed the Adhyātma;
he also composed the Nyāya, Vaiśeṣika, and Sāṃkhya systems along with the Īśvara doctrine. Īśvara was born from Puruṣa, and having been born, he composed the Atimārga.
The Pañcārtha, Lākula, and likewise the Pāśupata are considered [the five systems]. The Blessed Lord Sadāśiva also protected the Mantra-tantra.
Those things which were spoken, prohibited, and then spoken of again were [all] dependent [on one another].
The independent words of Śiva are manifold;
whatever has emerged from the upper stream is entirely infinite and so forth, as taught by that Supreme Lord to the high-souled Śrīkaṇṭha.

In the beginning, there existed a twofold knowledge according to the distinction of authority: that which reveals the Lord (pati), the fettered soul (pāśa), and the self (ātman) through the division of the supreme and the non-supreme;
the knowledge that illuminates Śiva is remembered as the supreme Śivajñāna.
The knowledge beyond the Vedas and other scriptures reveals the nature of the bound soul (*paśu*) and its fetters (*pāśa*);
just as the eye is useless for both men and women during the night,
so too is this dualistic knowledge distinct from that which is supreme and non-supreme (*parāpara*).
One should avoid a person who is devoted to the knowledge of astrology, whose mind is fixed on the Purāṇas, and who has exerted effort toward the goals of perfected beings (siddhas).

"One who, out of delusion, considers the Śaiva knowledge beginning with the Kāmika, as well as the knowledge of the meaning of the Vedas, to be equal— him one should avoid with effort. Again, in that same place:
The Gāruḍa, the Bhūtatantra, the Bhairava, the Vāmatantra, the Kāpāla,
the Pāñcarātra, the Lākula, the Kula-śāstra, the Pāśupata-tantra, and other Purāṇas, Dharma-śāstras, and Itihāsas.
And the six-limbed [Veda] known as Ṛg, Yajus, and Sāman;
likewise the Atharvaṇa, the Buddhist, and the doctrine of the Arhats;
from the scriptures arising from the upward stream (ūrdhvasrotas), through the sequence of the faces of Aparaśānta.
The Śiva-jñāna, beginning with the Kāmika, is always the head of the Blessed One; the others are indeed the heart, ears, and other limbs of Maheśa.
These have been declared here by Śambhu as the prima facie positions (pūrvapakṣa) for the sake of what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted.

In the *Vastrānirṇaya*, it is stated from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*) that "having set all those [other systems] aside, the Śiva-siddhānta has been proclaimed. Likewise, in the *Mahābhārata*, it is declared that the Vedas and other scriptures were composed by Śiva with specific intent (*sādhikaraṇa*).

"At the end of the Yuga, the great seers, permitted by Svayambhū himself, obtained through austerity the Vedas that were deficient in their interior portions, as well as the Itihāsas. And in the Vāyavīya Saṃhitā: "In this world, all the duties and stages of life (dharma-āśrama) are established for the sake of both [gods and men]."
Formerly fashioned by Brahmā, these two were preceded by my own command; that dharma of the Grandfather, however,
is accompanied by rituals requiring great wealth.

Not being endowed with that great dharma—which yields abundant ultimate fruit and is free from affliction—they find it exceedingly difficult to attain faith in the Great Ones. When their caste-status is obstructed, they take refuge in me alone, having no other resort. For them...
For the sake of dharma, desire, wealth, and liberation,
I have established the conduct of the castes and stages of life by an easy path. This is for my own devotees alone, even those who do not belong to any caste.

"The authority belongs to no others; thus, 'I am the ultimate Self'—this is the *tantra* for those humans who have fallen from the path of the Vedas. A *tantra* is not the Śiva-āgama [in that sense]. When it is so established, one should learn the Śiva-tantras from Śiva."

In the *Sambhava-kāṇḍa* of the *Skanda Purāṇa*, it is stated that Sanaka and others, as well as Śveta, Upamanyu, Kṛṣṇa, Arjuna, Mārkaṇḍeya, and others, have studied the Śiva Āgamas; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that their knowledge of matters not accessible to the Vedas would not have entered the path of their hearing, nor would they have been permitted by the Vedas [to know such things].

In the meantime, O Lord, on Mount Kailāsa, the Silver Mountain, the God remained [there] and related to Sanaka and the other lords of sages the Siddhānta known as the Rahasyāgama-nāma, which is commensurate with the meaning of the three categories (padārthas), as stated in the Upadeśakāṇḍa:
In ancient times, the four meritorious sons of Brahmā— Sanaka, Sanātana, the venerable Sanandana, and Sanatkumāra— performed the auspicious worship of Śambhu.
p. 1207) Then,
having taken refuge [in Śiva], the Vedas were indeed taught by Śiva to those of noble vows, as well as the Āgamas,
the Purāṇas, and the Itihāsas.
"Constantly devoted to the worship of Śiva, purified by the yoga of Śiva,
and having burned away the accumulation of great sins with the fire of the knowledge of Śiva"— thus it is stated in the *Śivapurāṇa*,
in the *Kāñcīpuramāhātmya*.
Sanatkumāra, with palms joined in reverence, questioned the Lotus-Seated One: "O Blessed One, all the Vedas, along with their limbs, sub-limbs, and compendiums,
as well as all the Śiva-āgamas, have indeed issued forth from your mouth."
In the *Skanda Purāṇa*, within the *Śvetāraṇya-māhātmya* and the *Puṇḍarīkapura-māhātmya*:
"Where in ancient times the great sage, the son of Vyāghrapāda, having bathed, reached the further shore of the Śiva-āgama,
which is difficult even for the gods to attain."
"That which has Kṛṣṇa as its disciple is remembered as the ninth sacred ford (tīrtha).
And in the Upadeśakāṇḍa:
"Furthermore, he who had assumed the form of Kṛṣṇa was born from the divine wife of Vasudeva."
Viṣṇu, whose nature is immeasurable, being summoned by the curse of Bhṛgu,
worshipped Mahādeva there, and having once again secured victory for Śakra, approached Upamanyu and was initiated according to that prescribed rite.
Then that preeminent devotee of Śiva, having worshipped Śaṅkara with devotion at that holy ford,
removed the burden of the earth and went to the world of Viṣṇu.
In that very place, there is this reply to Bāṇāsura:
He said to him: "O god, as before, you cannot now conquer me;
[I am protected] by the foremost of my devotees, the high-souled Upamanyu."

Having received initiation into Śiva, having drunk the essence of the Śiva-āgamas, and having attained the status of a Śaiva preceptor as well as supreme yoga, he reached the state of identity with Śiva;
by his name this forest is celebrated during the three daily rites, for it provides protection to that devotee.
"Named Śveta, he was devoted to men;
he had desisted from [worldly life] through his proficiency in the Śiva-āgamas, constantly wore the sacred ash, was full of vigor,
and endowed with devotion"— thus it is stated in that very same [text].

Having attained eternal life from the great sage Mārkaṇḍeya, he returned to his own home with supreme joy and remained devoted to his parents. He was peerless in the world, an expert in the scriptures of Śiva, and a master of the meaning of the Śivāgamas.
Even though one may exist as perfected in consciousness (*vijñāna*),
for human beings who have fallen from the path of revelation (*śruti*), this is the *tantra*; here,
"tantra" refers to the entire scripture that has emerged in the form of resonance (*nāda*).

The Śruti is not composed by Āśiva; rather, it should be understood by the wise that the Tantras such as the Vāmaka are composed by Māyārudra, impelled by the three Lords (Trirīśvara) and characterized by the state of Śambhu, consisting of the arrangement of phonemes, words, and sentences. As it is stated in the Kāmika:

"The Vāma, Pāśupata, Lākula, and Bhairava [systems] are not to be followed; they have been declared as outside the Vedas and otherwise [heterodox]. Furthermore, in the *Sūtasaṃhitā-vṛtti*, the venerable Vidyāraṇyasvāmin cites the Śivāgama.

"Even though he has accepted [the teaching], written it down, and been instructed by the Guru, he is devoid of connection with the Tantra"—in this context, "connection with the Tantra" (tantrasambandha) refers to... [p. 1209]

It has been explained that [the term] refers to being free from the production of scriptures contrary to the Vedas, such as the Kāpāla, Lākula, Vāma, and so forth. For instance, in the *Alāsya-māhātmya* within the *Vikrama-pāṇḍya-carita*, it is said that Pāṇḍya abandoned the scriptures outside the Vedas (*veda-bāhya-śāstra*).
The Śiva-śāstra has been heard;
Vedic dharmas have spread everywhere across the circle of the earth, while those who are outside the Vedas and follow improper traditions remain far removed from them.
"Always, with careful attention and great respect, he listens to the Śaiva scriptures, Purāṇas, and secret treatises from the mouths of the learned.
Likewise, the venerability of the Śivāgama is stated in the Vāyavīya Saṃhitā:
Speech devoted to my names is speech, not any other;

a body marked with the *tripuṇḍra* and other signs prescribed by my teaching, and intent on my service, is a body, not any other; [only] that which is known as the act of worshipping me [is true action].

External austerity is said to be that which consists of the emaciation of the body for my sake, such as the *kṛcchra* penances and the like; while internal austerity is the practice of the five-syllable mantra and the practice of the *praṇava*.

The practice of the Rudrādhyāya and so forth is not for the purpose of Vedic study; meditation is for the sake of contemplating my form and not for any other purpose; and the knowledge of the meaning of my scriptures is for the sake of realizing me and not for the sake of worldly wealth. Thus, as it is said:
Even if, in some way, [the self] possesses the characteristics of both generality and particularity,
liberation is undoubtedly attained through both of these paths of the Vedānta doctrine.

There is such attainment. This has been stated in the *Skanda Purāṇa*, in the *Cidambaramāhātmya*: "But those who are established in Vedānta, who are knowers [of reality] free from taint, who are devoted to my scripture, and who are grounded in the doctrines of knowledge..."
Both [traditions] likewise declare that union (sāyujya) is exceedingly difficult to attain,
whether through the paths devoted to ritual action (karma) or those devoted to Brahman—
both well-established in the Vedas and Āgamas— by which even sinners may abide; and they are of four kinds.

"Those who deserve punishment shall be punished as impelled by the scriptures," and "Both [the punisher and the punished] attain the extremely rare state of union (sāyujya)," according to the Śruti— this is the distinction.
Even for a Vedāntin who follows the established doctrine and knows the nature of Vedānta, [the path] is above Prakṛti.

Those who possess Śiva-initiation (śivadīkṣā) attain immediate union with Śiva (śivasāyujya) for the sake of liberation and for the knowledge of the categories of reality beginning with passion (rāga) and ending with the principle of Śiva (śivatattva), which are established solely through the Śiva-āgamas. In the absence of Śiva-initiation, even if one possesses knowledge of Vedānta, [liberation is not attained].
"They perceive it directly"— this has been stated in the *Sūtasaṃhitā*:
"Having established the disciple in the center of the pavilion, the Guru should again perform the severing of the knots by the very path prescribed by the Guru."
O best of the twice-born, when the compassionate Ācārya has thus acted, Mahādeva— the supreme among the greatly compassionate,
who is great bliss— impels his own innate, supreme, and virtuous Śakti; she, being gracious...
The Great Goddess, the supreme among those of great compassion,
is herself stainless within the conscious nature of the disciple's own self, [the nature] of Mahādeva.

O best of Brahmins, O twice-born ones, if a disciple is devoted and possesses devotion to the true Guru, then when his karma reaches equilibrium, the power of Śambhu falls intensely upon that disciple, who is a mass of consciousness.
For one endowed with such serenity, the knowledge arising from the Vedāntic statements burns away all ignorance within, just as the rising of the sun dispels darkness.
Even one who lacks the descent of grace (*śaktipāta*), provided he is truthful in speech and devoted to the guru, [attains realization] by hearing [the teachings] from the teacher.

One may be liberated from bondage through the sequence of Vedānta. A certain secret portion regarding the manner of the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) has not been told by me, both because of its secrecy and for fear of causing the king’s ruin.

In this regard, the distinction is as follows: Śakti, being the bestower through the descent of the rite of initiation (*dīkṣā*), first descends in a general form; subsequently, within the rite of initiation, she descends in a specific form, being directly of the nature of initiation itself. Thus she descends.

[The opponent says: "It is *śakti*. [The author replies: Therefore, the destruction of impurity (*mala*) does not occur through the Vedic path; for, according to the words of the *Devīmata*, "Liberation occurs only through initiation (*dīkṣā*) by means of the path taught in the Śaiva Āgamas," it burns away the ignorance consisting of the nature of impurity and the bonds (*mala-mauñjya-ātmikā-avidyā*) in due order for that duration of time.
Having reached the world of the principle of Puruṣa above Prakṛti, they enjoy great enjoyment; that is its purpose. This has been stated in the *Sarvajñānottara* and other texts:
"The [state] of those devoted to the Jina is characterized by Tamas, while that of the proponents of Brahman is Pauruṣa (pertaining to Puruṣa). For that which is non-existent, no knowledge exists."
Existence is not non-existence for that which is real;
therefore, this doctrine of a single self has been imagined by those with fundamental consciousness.

Thus, those who are possessed by the grasp of non-duality (advaita) are awakened by compassionate gurus who administer the medicine of the established doctrine (siddhānta). Even for those whose conduct is bound by chains,
having relied upon the power of non-duality— [their] non-duality...
"Dissolution occurs in the state of the Puruṣa as the ultimate goal;
those who know the Vedānta, the Sāṃkhyas, and the Yogins are established in the Puruṣa.
Thus it is said. Someone might somehow [claim] that the Śiva-āgamas are equal to the Veda in terms of being Brahman.
That gentleness which was mentioned is not ultimate; rather, gentleness is its very nature.
As it is stated in the *Kāmika*:
"Likewise, the Pāśupata, that called Soma-siddhānta, the Lākula, and the Gāruḍa..."
The Bhairava, Vāma, Bhūtatantra, and Yāmala;
the Kāpāla, Pāñcarātra, Bauddha, and likewise the Ārhata;
the Bṛhaspatimata, Sāṃkhya, Yoga, and likewise the Vaikhānasa.
The [text] called Vedānta, Mīmāṃsā, the Purāṇa-śāstra, the Vastu-śāstra, as well as the Sūtra, the Ṣaḍaṅga, and the Itihāsa— likewise,
whatever four deities were mentioned therein, all that is Raudra.
The peaceful Siddhānta is desired as that which has been taught;
and whatever has been established by the Rudras, such as the images of Viṣṇu and others— all that,
having rendered it Śaiva, the Śaiva practitioner should worship.
If a *liṅga* or other [object] established or worshipped by an Ādiśaiva is worshipped by them [the others], then indeed the kingdom and the king [suffer].
That village and all those residing in the village will perish, without a doubt. Sacrifice is declared to be of three kinds: superior, middling, and inferior.
Sacrifice performed solely with the mantras of Śiva shall be the superior one; [that performed] with Vedic [mantras], the Śiva...
Sacrifice performed with both [Vedic and Śaiva] mantras is middling;
sacrifice performed with Vedic mantras alone is inferior. One should perform sacrifice for one's own sake using Śaiva mantras alone as the best.
"There is no mantra equal to the Śaiva mantra in the three worlds," as stated in the *Buddhakāṇḍa* of the *Skanda Purāṇa*, in the chapter on the manifestation of Kumāra’s universal form:
"That entire web of sounds is situated in the region of the throat; in the middle of the mouth..."
The Vedas, O God, reside in the teeth of the god;
the syllables are in the teeth, while the Śiva-āgamas are on the tongue; and the seventy million great mantras are situated within the lips.
In the *Cidaṃbaramāhātmya*:
"Having thus summoned the gods, [he] circumambulated the city and the banner marked with the bull in the presence of the Lord of the Assembly."
They caused the tree to be planted according to the method prescribed in the Agamas.
In the Śiva Purāṇa, in the section on the greatness of Gaṅgā (*Gaṅgāmāhātmya*), it is said:
"Worship of Śiva is the foremost austerity, as described in the Vedas and Agamas; [it is] the perfection of austerity..."
"Pradasthāna, Puṇḍarīka, and Purammahat.
Thus [it is stated] in the *Śivapurāṇa*, in the section on the greatness of Ekāmranātha, within the context of Indra’s worship of Śiva (p.

"Vṛtraja propitiated the beloved of Kāmākṣī every day with vows, fire-offerings, recitations, and other rites prescribed in the Śiva Tantras," as stated in the Śiva Purāṇa, in the section on the Greatness of Viriñci.
"There was one named Śivanāyaka, the leader of the Śiva-brahmins,
who knew the meaning of the Kāmika and other Āgamas, appearing like Maheśvara himself. Thus it is stated in the *Śiva Purāṇa*, in the *Kālahastī Māhātmya*.
Having bathed in the Suvarṇamukharī river and recited the mantras pertaining to the Jāpāgama according to the prescribed rules for atonement, he,
with a serene soul and accompanied by the Brahmins,
worshipped the Lord according to the Tantra and returned once more to the penance grove.
In the Śaiva Purāṇa, within the Puṇḍarīka-māhātmya:
"He who, filled with fierce devotion, writes down the Śiva-śāstra and gives it to a Śiva-yogin,
shall attain union (sāyujya) with Śiva."
In the *Hālāsya-māhātmya*:
Having summoned the best of the twice-born, who were devoted to the banks of the Gaṅgā, the lord of the earth [invited them] for the sake of worshipping the Great Liṅga created by Śiva.

Having requested them, "May you worship the Great Liṅga continuously according to the Siddhāntas, beginning with the Kāmika," and having bestowed a livelihood upon them, Ceta [performed the rite] right there with the waters of the Gaṅgā-tīrtha from golden jars.
"Having gathered [the materials], he consecrated him with great festivity according to the rites prescribed in the Āgamas.
In the *Kuleśvara-vaibhava* section of the *Vedāraṇya-māhātmya*:
"They worshipped the Supreme Lord according to the path taught in the Āgamas."
"Maheśāna, Śaṅkara, the embodiment of nectar, adorned with the moon"—
thus [it is said] in the *Śivapurāṇa*, in the *Rāmeśvaramāhātmya*.

From that time forward, the Liṅga known as Rāmeśvara, honored by various mantras derived from the Āgamas and worshipped by Rāma, became widely renowned; thus was the etymological definition of the term "Āgama" and so forth explained in the Śubhadādikā.
That which came from the mouth of Śiva and went into the mouth of Girijā,
and which is the doctrine accepted by all the sages—
because it is that through which reality is attained, it is remembered as "Āgama" (the source). It expands [knowledge].
"Because it provides protection for men by relying upon vast purposes and the mantras of reality, it is known as *tantra*.
Thus ends the glorification of the Śiva-āgamas. It is indeed so.

The Śiva-śāstra, as it has been described, must be heard and studied by those alone who have received initiation (dīkṣita). For one devoid of initiation, however, all [attainment] such as knowledge (jñāna) and the rest would be in vain.
Since knowledge and the rest lack autonomy, they exist solely as ancillaries to initiation.

The means to liberation is not otherwise; as it has been said: "Its status as a constituent part [of that] occurs through initiation (dīkṣā), for initiation becomes the principal member. Apart from the singular initiation of Śiva, all other [means] are declared to be obstructed."
One is not liberated through knowledge, nor through yoga, nor even through conduct; for even in those [practices], the inherent capacity of knowledge and the rest is not found.
[This applies] to children, fools, the elderly, women, libertines, and likewise to the sick—[all of whom lack liberation] through knowledge and the rest.
"Therefore, there is no liberation; initiation alone is the liberator.
Regarding the claim that "liberation comes from knowledge alone," here too, the word "knowledge" [is used in a specific sense].
The meaning is precisely initiation (*dīkṣā*) and so forth.
As it is said in the *Suprabheda*:
"Now, therefore, I shall explain the section on knowledge (*jñānapāda*) in brief; at its beginning..."
Listen with a one-pointed mind to the creation of Śiva;
O child, knowledge proceeds for the sake of completely destroying all [bondage], for the destruction of the series of paths (adhvan),
and for bringing about the state of Śiva.

Ignorance is said to be like darkness, while knowledge is like a lamp; the object of knowledge is declared to be like the sun, after which knowledge itself perishes. Knowledge is said to be initiation and the like, which cuts through the nets of fetters.
The wise one takes recourse to the state of being the Lord of Paśus and Pāśas through knowledge;

there is no doubt that the attainment of absolute liberation (kaivalya) occurs through knowledge alone. Furthermore, initiation (dīkṣā) is the manifestation of the rite of initiation, which is itself moving.
The will of Śiva, assisted by the power of Śiva’s knowledge and consisting of power itself, is indeed the creative power (kriyā-śakti) of Śiva. This has been stated in the Parākhyatantra:
"The supreme initiation of the Lord, which brings about the destruction of merit and demerit, [arises] from knowledge..."
It is called such because of yoga and because of conduct;
and here, liberation for all living beings occurs through initiation. Therefore, by the power of Śiva, liberation is accomplished everywhere.
Likewise, in the *Skanda Purāṇa*, in the section concerning Bhṛgu’s curse: "No spiritual stage (*āśrama*) has been established by anyone; no excellence exists for men.

"Without the supreme initiation that liberates one from the three abodes of transmigration, there is no liberation; therefore, liberation is attained through initiation alone, not by the stages of life (āśramas) nor by other ritual acts. Thus it is stated in the Kāśī-khaṇḍa of the Skanda Purāṇa.
And just as men desiring liberation seek it without purification of the path,
or as one who is not a Caṇḍāla begins to go with a staff in hand,
or as those whose bodies are devoid of a boat desire to cross the ocean— so too is one devoid of purification of the path.
For he thus strives for liberation.
What is the use of saying much more here? Again and again I declare:
"The purification of the six paths" is taught in the venerable *Raurava*.
The *añjana* mantras are said to belong to those known as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Indra.

Having witnessed the supreme sovereignty of those great-souled Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśas*) and their yogic power, they became desirous of it and sought refuge in them. [Thus ends] the section on Knowledge (*vidyā*).
Those who are indifferent to everything ending with the title "Lord of Kings of Kings," who are discerning regarding the distinctions bound by the cycle of birth, old age, and death,
[attain their goal] through the pavilions of knowledge, initiations, sacrifices, offerings, and ritual acceptances.
And by means of instructions veiled by knowledge, and by the limbs of mantra and tantra that are free from defects— whether divine, non-divine, or otherwise, which illuminate those of pure being—
the auspicious Lords of Mantras (Mantrīśvaras) bestow grace upon them through fierce mantras.
And even their grandfathers and others, or those who were deluded by them, [attained] the supreme knowledge that is the cause of the highest liberation according to Śiva.
In accordance with the proper sequence, those who perform the great sacrifice of the King of Tantras bestow [the teachings] upon the sages, the wise, and the ancestors. Furthermore,
by the command of the Grandfather (Brahmā), the sages, their doubts severed, [received] the ritual of initiation (dīkṣā-vidhi).
Those who know the ritual procedures proclaim to humanity:
"This sūtra alone has issued forth from the rays of Śiva’s moon; it is the supreme means of illumination for the eggs of the darkness that is the flood of bonds."

In the Śiva Purāṇa, within the *Māhātmya* of Hemasabhānātha, Vyāghrapāda made him successful through the initiation of Śiva. Indeed, that Kanakavarman, by the grace of Vyāghrapāda, manifested a divine power obtained through the initiation of Śiva.
Śiva, whose conduct is like that of a humble man, having established firm devotion toward the Lord of the Tāṇḍava dance,
made his residence there. Furthermore, O King, in ancient times, nine hundred and ninety-nine sages also resided there.
Those who were initiated, together with us two, beheld the white Śiva-taṇḍava dance.
It is stated elsewhere:
"Just as an elephant in the forest, seeing a king, becomes terrified, so too [is one] regarding the worship performed by the uninitiated."
Having seen the *liṅga*, he was afraid, thinking it was Maheśvara.
In the Śiva Purāṇa:
"The uninitiated [practitioner] dwells in the armor of ritual rules and the fatigue of observances, yet remains devoid of mantra..."
"This worship of the All-pervasive Lord is not dependent upon ritual time-cycles.
Thus it is stated in the Gaṇeśvara-saṃhitā of the Śiva Purāṇa:
"Then, having established the Lord Nandin within his own self, [the devotee], with palms joined in reverence..."
Having prostrated like a staff upon the ground together with the gods, the Lord of Gaṇas caused Nandin to receive the initiation whose essence is Śiva, thereby pleasing him.
Again, in that very same place:
"They too were filled with wonder, delighted by the play of Śiva, thinking: 'We are blessed and have accomplished our purpose, since we have been initiated by Śiva himself.'"
In the *Ṣaṭsāhasrikā*:
"Through initiation one becomes fit for hearing [the teachings]; through initiation one is capable of performing worship;
through initiation, the duties of spiritual practice proceed according to their true purpose."
Through initiation (dīkṣā), knowledge is attained; through initiation, one becomes a possessor of supernatural powers (siddhi).
Initiation alone bestows liberation; it is the innermost factor in the acquisition of knowledge and other virtues.
Those who have been purified by the initiation of Śiva are qualified for everything; there is no [other requirement].
There is no sacred ford equal to initiation; there is no austerity equal to initiation;
there is no dharma equal to initiation; there is no quality equal to initiation;
there is no knowledge equal to initiation; there is no mindfulness equal to initiation.
"There is nothing to be known that is equal to initiation; there is no lineage (*kula*) equal to initiation.
And in the *Rauravasaṃgraha*:
"Having thus attained the Śaiva ritual path, which originates from initiation and mantra..."

"The initiated one, O best of men, undergoes rebirth. For by means of this, knowledge is indeed bestowed and the bondage of the fetters is destroyed; therefore, it is said in the Śiva-āgama that "initiation" (dīkṣā) is here truly a purificatory rite (saṃskāra).
"The true nature of knowledge is bestowed and the three impurities are destroyed;
because its essential nature is the destruction of [impurity] through knowledge, it is here called by the word 'initiation' (dīkṣā). (p. 1220)
In the *Varuṇapaddhati*, the various types [of initiation] are set forth:
"The initiation of sight and touch, as well as the verbal, the mental, the scriptural,
the initiation of yoga, the sacrificial initiation (*hautrī*), and so forth, in many ways."
Having meditated upon reality as if opening one's eyes, he gazes at the disciple;
this initiation by the eye (akṣuṣī-dīkṣā) serves to liberate him from the bonds of the fetters (pāśa).
Then, having placed Śiva, complete in all his limbs, upon the right hand...
One should touch the head and other parts of the disciple; this becomes the initiation by touch (*sparśadīkṣā*).
Having concentrated the mind upon reality with an expanded inner consciousness, one should utter the *saṃhitā* mantras; this is proclaimed as the verbal initiation (*vāgdīkṣā*).
Relying upon the mental rite, the initiation is performed mentally;
through the transmission of the scripture, it is proclaimed as scriptural initiation (śāstradīkṣā);
through yoga, it is the initiation of yoga (yogadīkṣā), firmly established in the state of Śiva. This is initiation (dīkṣā).
Those associated with the Tāmisra [hell] and called "attendants" (paricāra) are not fit for the worship of the Liṅga, much less for rites such as initiation (udīkṣā);
for they remain established in the conventional [world], being devoid of the elevation of their caste (jātyuddhāra).
In the northwest— [it is said]:
"For false Śūdras, those of the lowest castes, and especially for artisans,
as well as for those of mixed castes, the purification of the path (adhvaśuddhi) is not prescribed."

In this regard, for one born in the natural order (anuloma) and united with those such as the twice-born, the purification of the path and other rites for them should be performed according to what is appropriate for the mother's lineage.

In the *Suprabheda*, six [types of initiation] are declared to be in direct order (*anuloma*) and three in reverse order (*pratiloma*); each of these three is further divided into three kinds. The intermediate types (*antarāla*) are for the application of all [initiations] in the ritual act of initiation (*dīkṣākarma*).
"All Vrātyas are to be abandoned, excluded from all ritual acts. In the *Kiraṇa*:
"Because of that [impurity], even for an outcaste (antyaja), initiation is indeed mental; but for artisans..."
One should not entertain improper thoughts due to physical contact;
having recognized their supreme devotion, if one acts out of greed, one incurs fault.
Thus it is said in the Vāyavya [Purāṇa].

If these [devotees] possess genuine devotion toward Śiva, the supreme cause, one should effect the purification of their bonds through the offering of water from his feet and other such acts. Furthermore,
elsewhere:

One who does not drink intoxicants, is of noble birth, and is constantly devoted to dharma should be known as equal to a Śūdra-Kṣatriya; the rest are far inferior to him. For those devotees, there shall be no initiation for the office of the Hotṛ priest, nor the Ākṣuṣīmatī [initiation].
In the *Vāruṇapaddhati*, a distinction regarding the *hautrī* is stated: "The *hautrī* who possesses the dust [of the ritual ground] like a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍavatī*) is said to be of two kinds;
indeed, initiation is held by those who know this to be of two types here."

One is known as "possessing knowledge" (jñānavatī) and the other as "possessing ritual action" (kriyāvatī). Initiation that consists merely of mental activity—such as worship, fire-offerings, and ritual acts—is declared to be "possessing knowledge," for it brings about the correct awakening to reality; whereas [initiation] possessing fire-offerings is [the one possessing ritual action].
But that ritual action which arises from skillfulness is manifold;
it is both with seed and without seed.
As stated in the *Kālottara*:
Initiation (*dīkṣā*) is said to be "action-oriented" (*kriyāvatī*) for the four castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇa;
furthermore, it is said to be threefold as "priestly" (*hautrī*) in the *Vāmana*.
In the Śiva-āgama, initiation (dīkṣā) is taught by Śiva, the Supreme Self, as being threefold: Śāmbhavī, Śāktī, and Māntrī.
[The teacher is one] who possesses the vision of the knowledge of reality from the tip of the nose up to the trident.
By the mere sight of the Guru, or even through touch and conversation,
that which immediately brings about the destruction of bonds arises here;
that is declared to be the Śāmbhavī initiation, and it is further divided into two kinds.

And it is classified as intense (*tīvra*) and more intense (*atīvratarā*) according to the degree of the destruction of the fetters (*pāśa*). That by which immediate liberation (*nirvṛti*) occurs is considered the "more intense" (*tīvratarā*).
The "intense" (*tīvra*), however, is the power of Śakti (*śāktī*) which eternally purifies both merit and demerit for one who lives.

The initiation consisting of knowledge (*jñānavatī dīkṣā*) is performed by the Guru, having entered the body of the disciple through the path of yoga and with the eye of wisdom. The initiatory rite consisting of mantra (*māntrī dīkṣā*) and consisting of ritual action (*kriyāvatī dīkṣā*) is preceded by the sacrificial pit and the pavilion.
The Guru should perform the initiation outside [the mandala] with very gentle and slow instruction, either through knowledge or through ritual action. "The Guru should purify the disciple;
if he performs it otherwise out of delusion, that evil-minded one perishes. One [initiation] is possessed of knowledge.
The second [initiation] is called *kriyāvatī*;
this has been extracted and stated again in the venerable *Cintyaviśvasādākhya*.
Thus, one who has attained the initiatory rite (*māntrī-kriyā-dīkṣā*) is the most excellent of those possessing qualities; he alone—
And one is qualified for the initiation into Yoga (*yogadīkṣā*) in no other way.
1223) For disciples who are already endowed with a previous initiation, the *āṇava* [initiation] is the most excellent; [then follows] the *śākta*...
The Śāmbhava initiation is threefold:
it is performed by me according to reality as the Śākta and the Śāmbhava;
whereas the Āṇava initiation is performed by others according to the distinctions of dull, intense, and so forth—thus it has been stated.
Even by other gurus who possess the power of yoga, a ritual initiation (*kriyādīkṣā*), though performed more slowly,

is sufficient for one who is "over-ripe" [in spiritual maturity] or poor; or else, there is the extraction of the *Prāsāda* mantra uttered immediately through the procedure of initiation, even when there is a deficiency in the mantras and so forth.

The meaning also flashes forth within that [text]: "Having effected the union with Śiva, the emergence of the six secrets, and the manifestation of Śiva-nature; being composed of the essence of the mantras beginning with *satva* and so on, she is contracted together with the Śākta and Śāmbhavī [powers], and thus the auxiliary [means] is also included."

Therefore, one who is devoid of these three types of initiation is a *paśu* (bound soul). As it has been said: "A Brahmin who upholds the four Vedas but is bereft of Śiva-initiation is like the water of the Bhāgīrathī in the vessels of wicked Cāṇḍālas."

"O Śūdra, even for one who has pacified ten million Brahmins and is endowed with the initiation of Śiva, the knowledge of Śiva is very difficult to attain, and its practice is even more difficult to attain. Knowing this to be very difficult to attain, one should practice devotion toward Śiva."
Thus ends the greatness of Śiva-initiation.
Therefore, the Śiva-śāstra is to be studied only by those of the four castes who have been initiated with Śiva-initiation (śivadīkṣā). As it is stated in the Suprabheda:
"Excellent, excellent, O one of great wisdom, that which has been requested by you!"
This *Śuddhaśaiva* *Idantatra* is not to be given away nor made public; it is to be imparted only to one who is initiated,
steadfast, and supremely devoted to Śiva.
Indeed, it is praised that one should not speak of this elsewhere except to those worthy of hearing it. Through initiation, one should lead the four types of pure Śaivas to Śiva.
Now hear how everyone should conduct themselves according to the path of worldly custom: study...
Teaching, officiating at sacrifices, performing sacrifices oneself, giving gifts, and receiving gifts— these are said to be their duties. Furthermore,
the Kāmika and other Āgamas are declared here to be manifestly identical with Śiva.

Their very studies are said to be his study; their very acts of teaching are indeed his teaching. Through the worship of Śiva, his own sacrifice and officiating at sacrifices for others are likewise accomplished.
Whatever substance is given with Śiva in view, that gift itself,
or the acceptance of it by one who possesses [the lineage], is called the sixfold action (ṣatkarma) of the wise, pure Śaiva who is endowed with the true being of Śiva.
In the *Makuṭa*:
"This unsurpassed tantra is to be given to the Śiva-yogins who have been initiated into nirvāṇa; it must not be given to others."
And in the *Kāñcīpuramahātmya*:
"A Brāhmaṇa who is learned in the Vedas, a devotee of Śiva, one who has conquered his senses,
endowed with sacred ashes and rudrākṣa beads, and solely intent upon the worship of Śiva."
One who is devoted to the thorough knowledge of the meaning of the scriptures and follows the auspicious dharma—
whether he be a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or even a Śūdra of inverse birth (pratiloma)— provided he is stainless.
Or even one born in the lineage, who directly takes refuge in Āmreśa—
by means of devotion, according to one's wealth, with houses, fields, riches, and so forth— one should cause him to dwell there.
Whatever fruit is proclaimed for the installation (*pratiṣṭhā*) of the deities, that same fruit [is obtained by this].
"Having obtained it in its entirety, one is liberated from the ocean of existence. Thus it is said in the Śaiva Purāṇa:
"This [knowledge] indeed [should be given] to a devotee of Śiva who has studied the scriptures of Śiva..."
"O bull among sages, this should be revealed to one who has been purified by the initiation of Śiva.
Likewise, in the *Kiraṇavṛtti*, the venerable teacher Rāmakaṇṭha states:
"It is understood that for him, those very [initiations] have resulted in the initiation of liberation (*nirvāṇadīkṣā*)."

Having begun by stating that "those who have not been initiated have no entitlement to hear [this]," he will say, "When all men have attained... and so forth; here, the word "all" refers to Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, Mlecchas, and others, for they too are indeed eligible according to the Śruti.
This has been explained according to the sequence of the chapter on the Guru-nature, because every word has an indefinite meaning.
Now, it might be asked: "Should this be recited by those devoid of initiation? To this, it is said in the *Kāmika*:
If Brahmins and the other three castes who are devoid of initiation, as well as those of Śūdra birth,
should study the Śiva-śāstra, the kingdom and its ruler will perish.
(Cintyaviśva):
One should never impart the knowledge of Śiva nor write it down for one initiated by a Brahmin or others;
moreover, one must especially not study it in the presence of one who is uninitiated.
In the Vīra-tantra it is said: "It should be heard by those initiated into the channels (nāḍī-dīkṣita), but it must not be given nor revealed [to others].
It should indeed be given to disciples; I shall tell this to you in brief."
And elsewhere it is said:
"A wise man should not, with effort, impart the knowledge of Śiva to an animal (paśu); nor should he engage in study in the vicinity of animals."
Even among the four castes, only those who have been initiated are superior.
As it is said in the Śaiva Purāṇa:
"The status of a Śūdra has departed from the Śūdra, and the status of a twice-born has departed from the Brāhmaṇa."

Due to the connection with the Śiva-saṃskāra, no distinction of caste exists. For one who is born from the Śiva-initiation (śivadīkṣā), one should not contemplate a previous birth; just as there is no prior mental conception regarding a consecrated Liṅga.
In the Śivadharmottara:
"The Liṅga is held to be of two kinds: stationary and mobile. They know the stationary Liṅga to be the installed one, and the mobile one to be the initiated [soul]."
"By disparaging the *jaṅga*, the installation becomes fruitless; therefore, a wise person should never disparage the two *liṅgas*.
Thus it is stated in the venerable *Mataṅga*.
Those who desire Śiva should look upon the devotees of Śiva as if they were Śiva himself.
Having been consecrated by the guru— the embodiment of the mantra— with Śiva-mantras,
those men have obtained all boons and are born from the womb of Vāgīśī, just as it has been described.
"Those whose bodies have been purified by the Śiva-saṃskāra are all equal in their dharma; nevertheless, it is ordained thus.
In the *Kāmika*:
"Through contact with fire, fuel no longer bears the name of 'tree'; the Śūdra-status of a Śūdra has passed away, and the twice-born-status of a Brāhmaṇa [is attained]."
"Due to the connection with the Śiva-consecration (śivasaṃskāra), no distinction of caste exists.
And elsewhere:
"Gold, silver, copper, and iron—this quartet undergoes [transformation]."
The state of being gold [is attained] through the power of the penetration by mercury;
just as copper perfected by mercury does not again become copper,
so too a person perfected by bhāna does not again become a śūdra.
Just as water contained within a mother-of-pearl shell certainly becomes a pearl— yet it does not again become water, nor does it ever abandon its state as a pearl—
as stated in the *Jñānalakṣaṇasamuccaya*:
"How can he who has Śiva as his father— Vyomavyāpin— and Vāgīśī as his mother,
having been born through mantras in the Śiva-sacrifice, be a Śūdra?
Just as the notion that jars and other objects are made of clay never arises again once they have undergone consecration (saṃskāra), so too [is this case]."
Furthermore, due to the abandonment of the bonds, the ordinary castes of men do not exist;
nor would the state of Śiva-hood be known through the Śiva-consecration. In that case, there would certainly be no teachers such as the twice-born, the gods, and so forth.
"Refined by the guru through mantra-purification and initiation, the entire universe of moving and non-moving beings certainly attains the state of Śiva at that very moment.
Thus it is stated in the *Cintyaviśva*:
Like a sinner who perceives a stone in a Śiva-liṅga,
he possesses excellence, especially through his desire for liberation, he whose mind—
One should not remember his birth and so forth when he is absorbed in Śiva.
Whether it be silver, copper, lead, or iron,
once it has been pierced by means of pills and the like, one should likewise lead those who have been initiated [into that state].
The prior form, the name, the mark, its designation, and the differentiator— all these attain equality once the nature of gold is established. As stated in the *Kāmika*:

Even those of the Brāhmaṇa and other castes may become Śūdras; therefore, one should uplift them by their virtues. Having uplifted the Śūdra caste from its very root with the [mantra] ending in "svāhā," as stated in the *Skandakālottara*:
O Six-faced One, one should perform the *jātyuddharaṇa* oblation, burning each individual of the Śūdra caste by the hundreds with fire;
having thus established them in the status of a true Śūdra, perform the sixteen rites.
"Once he has directly attained the state of a Brahmin, you should then perform the initiation;
one should cause the members of the three higher castes to do so according to this rule. Thus it is stated in the *Kāmika*.

"Salutation (namaḥ) and vauṣaṭ [are used] for a Śūdra, [the mantra] being devoid of the Praṇava and other [prefixes]. However, one who has been initiated into Nirvāṇa may join it with the Praṇava. And in the Makuṭa [Tantra]:
"One should employ the Pradhāna in one initiated for Nirvāṇa," as stated in the Suprabheda:
"For ascetics who are pure Śaivas, whose nature is that of mortals devoted to Maheśvara..."
One should offer a special meal there according to one's ability.
Even if they are not initiated, those who are devotees of Śiva— even if they are other than liberated devotees— are indeed superior.
The characteristics of a devotee of Śiva are stated in the Upadeśakāṇḍa: "There are some among the gods, among the Daityas, and among the Yātudhānas who possess the majesty of devotion to Śiva."
Among yakṣas, gandharvas, and bhogins;
among lords of sages, mortals, brahmins, and kings; and even among those born of the thighs [vaiśyas], śūdras, and all types of mixed castes—everywhere.
O lords of men, they have no established system of castes and stages of life;
indeed, they all possess only the form of Maheśvara.
They are declared in all the Vedas to be "beyond the castes and stages of life" (ativarṇāśrama) and the most excellent of beings.
In the Vāyavyasaṃhitā: "Thus, he in whom these eightfold marks exist, even if he be a barbarian (mleccha), is the best of Brahmins, an illustrious sage, an ascetic, and a scholar."

"To one who is beloved, learned in the four Vedas, and my devotee—even if he is a cook—to him gifts should be given and from him [gifts] should be accepted; and he is to be honored just as I am. Thus it is said in the Vāsiṣṭha-laiṅga.

"Even if a Caṇḍāla should constantly utter the word 'Śiva' with joy, he does not tolerate the speech of the Vedas, nor does he tolerate [the company of] the virtuous, nor shall he dwell [among them]. And in the *Vṛddhācalamāhātmya*:
Whether he be a learned man, a preeminent ascetic, or even a dog-cooker, if he is devoted, he alone is worthy;
no other is to be honored, even if he upholds the four Vedas. One should give to him, for he is the very form of Śiva.
(From the Upadeśakāṇḍa)
"Even for the most wicked person, there is indeed liberation if they wear sacred ash and rudrākṣa beads"—
thus it is stated everywhere in the Vedas, Purāṇas, and Āgamas as well.
"It is counted in many ways in the world by all great-souled ones.
And the characteristic of devotion is stated in the *Sūtasaṃhitā*:
"O observer of noble vows, for those who are solely devoted to the knowledge of Śiva, [devotion is absent] toward one who reviles that knowledge of Śiva."
The severing of one's head is understood as devotion to Śiva;
the transcription of the Śiva-vidyā and the offering of the book are declared to be devotion to Śiva by those learned in the Śiva scriptures.
In the *Kiraṇa*:
"Food fit for consumption belongs to three [classes], but never ending with the Śūdra. Those Śūdras who are endowed with purity and right conduct and are not drinkers of intoxicants are auspicious."
"Supreme devotees of Rudra are fed even the objects of enjoyment.
Thus ends the *Śivabhaktamāhātmya*.
In the Kāmika:
"I shall declare the determination of the lineages (gotra) for all the sages as well; two kinds of lineage are mentioned here: that arising from initiation and likewise that born of birth."
Kauśika— Kāśyapa, Bharadvāja, Gautama, Agastya, Atri, Vasiṣṭha, and Jamadagni Bhārgava.
Aṅgiras and Manu—the first—have been proclaimed as being of two kinds:
those sages who are endowed with Śiva’s creation and those who are devoid of it.
These [latter], however, are possessed of Śiva’s creation and have been initiated into the five faces by Śiva.
The twice-born born into that lineage are Śaivas who belong to the lineage of the peaceful ones (sāntānika);
they are to be known as the Ādiśaivas, remembered as the bestowers of grace upon all.
In the *Suprabheda*:

"For initiated twice-born men who are *anuloma* (of mixed but valid caste), [the rite] is for their own sake; for those who follow the primary Śaiva [tradition], it is for the sake of others; for others, it should be for both their own sake and the sake of others."
In the Kāmika:
"If ordinary Brahmins worship Śiva for the sake of a livelihood, they fall after six months; therefore, one should avoid them."
For a wise Śiva-brahmin who has been purified by Śiva-initiation,
performing sacrifices for the sake of others under the authority of Śiva’s command incurs no fault.
— [In the section on] Artisanry (Śilpa):
O Śaiva, the worship of Śiva is the worship of the twice-born devotees of Śiva, and that of Viṣṇu is the worship of those who maintain the sacred fires (vaidhānasa).
If a Brahmin should worship others in such a manner, they call him a Caṇḍāla or a temple-priest (devalaka). Elsewhere it is said:
If one who is uninitiated worships Brahmins for six months, they fall from their status after those six months; he is indeed known as a *devalaka*. (In the *Vīratantra*):
For the sake of worldly prosperity, one who follows the Śaiva path should always worship Śiva at the prescribed times;
and that worship, consisting of the performance of one's own duty, does not lead to any fault.
One who is uninitiated, even if he is a master of the four Vedas, must not touch the Śivaliṅga; nor should one who is [only] initiated...
A Brahmin should not perform worship for the sake of a livelihood;
he should perform worship for his own sake, and never for the sake of another. As stated in the Vīra-tantra:

One who is uninitiated, even if he knows the four Vedas, should not perform the worship of Śiva. Even when chosen, those who perform the worship while devoid of the prescribed rites fall within six months; they are indeed known as *devalakas*. Three...
If a consecrated Brahmin remains for years at shrines for the sake of a livelihood and performs worship, he is indeed remembered as a *devalaka*.
In the *Śaivaratnākara*:
"If a Brahmin who has been initiated— even one who is a master of the four Vedas—
should touch a Liṅga, or if it should be touched by a dog," [it becomes defiled].
If an uninitiated Brahmin performs the worship of a Liṅga, he becomes a Brahma-rākṣasa dwelling in a waterless forest region.
One who has mastered the four Vedas should worship the Śiva-liṅga; [he shall rule] over the kingdom and the nation.
His village perishes;
he who first worships here is remembered as a *devalaka* by all.
— From the *Yogaja*.

An initiated master of the four Vedas may perform worship for the sake of others until its conclusion. Even a Brahmin who has not been initiated, if he touches Śiva for six months in succession, he too becomes a *devālaka*.
He is declared unworthy for the worship of the gods.
Even a Brahmin who, having been initiated, worships the Lord of Gods for three years for the sake of a livelihood,
he too becomes a *devalaka*.
In the *Makuṭa*:
"Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and those who have been initiated are the ones who enter.
One may perform a sacrifice for one's own sake, but one must not perform it for the sake of another."
Aṃśumatī said:
"Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and even Śūdras who have been initiated may perform sacrifices for their own sake, but they must not perform them for the sake of others."
The worship of women born of the four castes is especially significant.
In the *Kāmika*:
"To Śiva, to the auspicious ones, and to the Brahmins, one should give a cow along with a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) consisting of ten *niṣkas*."
For that purpose, or for that purpose, or even just a *niṣka* [of gold];
in that very [text]— (p. 1233) —it says:

A Śiva-brahmin must always perform sacrifices for the sake of others; he is declared to be a righteous, eternal devotee of Śiva, and the best among the twice-born. If others were to act thus for their own sake, it would lead to the destruction of the performer. [This applies to] the creation of Śiva.

Those who are born from the mouth of Brahmā without [the study of] that [Veda] are neither commoners nor do they possess the qualification for performing rites for the sake of others; if they should perform them out of delusion,
it results in the destruction of the king and the kingdom.
In that very same [text]:
"Therefore, a Śiva-brāhmaṇa should perform sacrifices for others as well as for himself;
however, for others, it is indeed only for their own sake."
If one should act for the sake of another out of greed, then there will be no doubt that the destruction of the king who witnesses it will occur before long.
In that very same [text]:

He who, even upon seeing an action contrary [to dharma], maintains indifference, that king attains imperishability; there is no need for further deliberation. Therefore, by the preeminent teacher who abides within the five spheres of perception, there is the thorough knowledge of the Śaiva Āgamas.
By one who has reached the further shore and is engaged in action—
action being performed for the sake of the prosperity of his own kingdom—
in that very [text]:
Rituals for pacification (*śāntika*) and nourishment (*pauṣṭika*) should not be performed by kings, especially those involving malevolent magic (*ābhicāra*) and the like against others.

However, such rites may be undertaken by one who is devoted to righteousness (*dharmaniṣṭha*) and intent on the continuity of his lineage; indeed, it is by such a person that they should be practiced.
It always grants the fulfillment of actions for men;
in that very [text]— (p. 1234) —it says:
It must be performed by an Ādiśaiva and especially not by others; if it is performed by others, it will be fruitless for him. In that very same [text]:

Any non-white (black) rite that should be performed for oneself or for others— including the installation [of an image] and the sacrifice— should belong to the Ādiśaiva and other such traditions. Any rite performed by another is known as *ābhicāra* (malevolent magic).
