If that which has been performed is done otherwise, it indeed leads to malevolent magic (*ābhicāra*). Just as a cow does not produce milk for another's calf, so too [the rite] will not yield its essence.
Therefore, one should have it performed with every effort by one who is established in Śaivism.
In the Yoga-born [tantra],
the installation and the sacrifice belong to the Ādiśaiva; any rite performed by another is known as *ābhicāra*.
In that very same [text]:
"The rites beginning with installation and ending with worship must be performed by an Ādiśaiva; he who causes them to be performed otherwise shall obtain only the Niṣkala."

In the *Suprabhedatantra*, regarding the *Caryāpāda*, that which is not mentioned there should be practiced according to the general rule; having observed that in the *Bodhāyanasūtra*, one should perform the ritual action.
Therefore, the Sūtra for them was proclaimed by Bodhāyana; these are declared to be the Ādi-Śaivas, though this has been stated in brief and not in detail. (From the Yogaja)
He is called Ādiśaiva; that Śiva-like Brāhmaṇa is the Guru. Deśika and Sthāpaka are indeed synonyms for him. Because he was a Śaiva from the very beginning, he is remembered as Ādiśaiva.
Because he has been initiated by Śiva, he is called a Śiva-brāhmaṇa; and because he is the teacher of all,
he is designated as the Guru.
He by whom the place and so forth are indicated is known as the *deśika* (guide). Because of his fitness for the installation of the *liṅga*, he is designated by the name *sthāpaka* (installer).
In that very same [text]:

He who is called Ādiśaiva is the Śiva-brāhmaṇa preceptor. Those to be initiated by an Ādiśaiva are not merely Anuśaivakas; rather, among Brāhmaṇas they are Mahāśaivas, and among kings they are Anuśaivakas. Among ordinary men—
The Bhoga-Śaiva and the Antara-Śaiva are for the Śūdra;
among the various types of Śaivas, beginning with the Ādi-Śaiva, the Ādi-Śaiva shall be the Guru.
As stated in the Kāmika:

One born into a family of the Ādiśaiva lineage is the most excellent for performing installations and other rites. Furthermore, among all mortals— whether they be Brahmins or members of the other four castes— whoever is engaged in their own specific duty during initiation, consecration, or festival [is likewise qualified].
He who is engaged in bathing, sprinkling, other rites of atonement, and consecration;
in the rejection [of offerings] and so forth, whether for his own sake or for the sake of others;
and in the worship of all the gods—he is considered a Guru of the Ādiśaiva tradition.
In the *Makuṭa*:
"Regarding the initiation of the four castes, the specific rule is that the Brāhmaṇa is the preceptor; the initiated Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras are those who enter [the mandala]."

One should perform sacrifice for one's own sake, but not for the sake of others; however, by an adherent of the Upper Śaiva (Ūrdhvaśaiva), it should be performed both for one's own sake and for the sake of others.
The one above is called Śaiva; he is the Brāhmaṇa Guru, Śiva himself.
In the Kāraṇa, O Prajāpati, five Śaivas are enumerated, while in the Siddhānta, the first—
One who is not an Ādiśaiva is not truly a Śaiva; rather, Sadāśiva is the true Śaiva.
The second type is the Ādiśaiva, who is said to have Śiva as his very essence. One who was initiated by Sadāśiva himself at the beginning is indeed an Ādiśaivaka.
Kauśika, Kāśyapa, Bharadvāja along with Gautama, and Agastya—
these five were initiated into the five faces.
Kauśika was initiated into the domain of Śiva by means of the form of Śiva himself.
Kārya was initiated by Īśvara alone, established within the sphere of Śiva;
Bharadvāja was initiated by Īśāna, [established] within the sphere of Jyotis; and Gautama is remembered as having been initiated by the form of Brahmā, [established] within the sphere of Sāvitrī.
Agastya, initiated with an upward-facing mouth, became a wanderer of the sky. This is proclaimed as the domain of the five sages.
These are declared to be the Ādi-Śaivas; their domain is called the Kula. Those born within these Kulas...

The performers of rites such as installation are the *raṅgaka*s; these initiators are known as the *ādiśaiva*s. But the third is the *mahāśaiva*, who is called a *vipra* belonging to the *śaiva* [tradition].
The fourth is known as Anuśaiva, while the King (Kṣatriya) and the Vaiśya are considered Kṛta.
The fifth is called Uttaraśaiva, and the Śūdra is said to be Sva.
Śiva is declared to be Anāśrita (the Unsupported), and those who depend upon him are the Ādiśaivas (the Primary Śaivas).
The Ādiśaivas are said to be those who rely on the Matas and the Anuśaivas; [this is stated] in the Svāyaṃbhuvatantra. (p. 1237)
In the established doctrines, the five Śaivas are proclaimed as having four faces: the first is the Anādi-Śaiva,
the second is the Ādi-Śaiva,
the third is the Mahā-Śaiva, and the fourth is the Anu-Śaivaka.

Now, Kṛṣṇa, you shall be told in due order about the Āntaraśaiva; that which was taught by Śiva is called Ādiśaiva, and one who has taken refuge in that is an Ādiśaiva. Those initiated into the beginningless and primordial [tradition] are the Ādiśaivas.

But others, such as the Mahāśaivas and so forth, are those who enter among the Brahmins and the rest; O Four-faced One, because they have attained the state of Śiva upon entering here, they are called "Praveśakas" (those who enter), just as one is called a "lepanaka" (anointer) or a "tāmrava" (copper-smelter). Thus they are known as Praveśakas.
The names [of the tantras] are common to the ends [of the vehicles]; in the *Suprabheda*:
"For the destruction of the impurities of beings, for their very sake, for the purpose of worshipping the Supreme, and for the awakening of others."
And for the purpose of performing the rites of installation, sprinkling, and initiation,
those who were created by Śiva— the Supreme Self— and not by anyone else, are the Śaivas. From the mouth of Brahmā, they have descended in succession to the mortal world, [starting] from Kāśī...
They were proclaimed by the sages and gods known as the Pādikas;
because they possess the state of Śiva from the very beginning (ādi), they are called Ādiśaivas. Those who have been initiated by Śiva are remembered as Śivabrāhmaṇas.
The supreme teachers, together with Vyoma, the most excellent of Brahmins, the highest of Śivas,
the best among the best of the twice-born, Śivaśveta, and those whose very nature is Śiva— of them...
The synonymous names have been told to you in brief.
In that very same [text] it says:
"Now I shall speak of the Anuśaivas; these initiated Brāhmaṇas are indeed the Anuśaivas."
The sequence has been stated, and now hear about the end (*anta*).
The three castes beginning with the Kṣatriya are designated as *antastha* Śaivas.
Through the *ādiśaiva* or *anuśaiva* [initiations], initiation is accomplished in due order.
Thus, the characteristics of the Antara-Śaivas have been briefly described. For those Antara-Śaivas, the Anu-Śaiva shall be the guru;
and for those Anu-Śaivas, the Ādi-Śaiva shall be the guru. [This applies] to all of them.

He who is called Guru is Śiva, the White One (Śveta), whose very nature is auspiciousness (Śivātmaka). Formerly, he was born from the mouths of Brahmā as Śveta; thereafter, the Śvetas were born, who are known as the common Śvetakas.
Those who were born on earth as Brāhmaṇas from the four mouths of Brahmā through the creation of Śiva are known as Śiva-Brāhmaṇas;
for they are not born merely from the mouth [of Brahmā] alone, but rather through the creative power of Śiva. These are the ordinary [Brāhmaṇas].
The Brahmins should lead them to Śiva by means of initiation.
In that very same [text]:
"Then, however, one should initiate those beginning with the Brahmins according to their respective order."

One who possesses the characteristics of an Ācārya, is well-versed in the Śiva Siddhānta, is a true Ādiśaiva, is well-integrated, and is the most excellent of all gurus— thus it is stated in the Vīrāgama.
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras, as well as those initiated by teachers,
may perform sacrifices for their own sake; however, they must not perform sacrifices for the sake of others.
Regarding those born of yoga— the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras who have been initiated and are worshippers—
they may perform sacrifice for their own sake, but they must not perform it for the sake of others.
Regarding the subtle [level]:

sacrifice is traditionally held to be of two kinds—performed for one's own sake and for the sake of others. Among these, sacrifice performed for one's own sake is praised for those such as the twice-born who observe the Śiva-vow.
It is said that for the sake of others, Śivadvija, born in the noble land (Āryadeśa),
[performed] the cause— [namely] the Mahā-... and likewise the Anuśaivas and the Antaraśaivas.
One may perform a sacrifice for one's own sake, but not for the sake of others; as stated in the *Suprabheda*:
"For initiated twice-born men and others of the same caste, [the rite] is for their own sake."
The worship for the sake of others belongs to the Ādiśaivas, while that for one's own self [belongs to the Siddhāntins].
In that very same [text]:
"Now, therefore, I shall fully declare the characteristics of the Ācārya and the procedure for the ripening of the fruit."
When, having understood this, devotion to Śiva arises, one proceeds with the installation of the *puṃlinga* and the *aliṅga*. First, one should seek out an Ācārya, and after that, the Mūrtipās.

One born of the Kula of the primordial Śaivas, established in the five spheres of perception, knowing the true meaning of all scriptures, and proficient in the knowledge of Śiva— such a learned man as this, who should perform the installation and other rites, he alone is the *sthāpaka* (the installer).
O child, none other than the All-pervading Lord [is the true deity];
one should never perform the installation (sthāpana) and other rites for those who follow Anuśaiva and similar traditions.
For the rites of installation and so forth must be performed by a practitioner of Ādiśaiva.
Otherwise, however, that [act] would be nothing but a transgression against the command of the Creator; for the Lord of Gods does not accept it,
since it does not arise from [the attainment of] its fruit.
In that very place— [he should honor] those endowed with the limbs of the primary Śaiva [tradition], who know the ritual procedures, who are joined with mantras,
who observe the Śiva-vow, who are preeminent, and who are experts in the Śaiva deities.

Having invited one hundred and eight Ādiśaivas, or even just a few, one should have all the rites, beginning with the installation, performed by the Ādiśaiva. Being impelled by the injunctions of the ritual, one should likewise cause initiation (*dīkṣā*) and authorization (*ājñā*) to be conferred upon them all.
In the Kāmika:

"One should commence the rite of Homa together with those who bear the form of the Guru; [the officiant] should be adorned with the ornaments previously mentioned and born of a lineage originating from Ādiśiva."
In that very same work, in the *Gaurī-kalyāṇa-paṭala*:
"One born of a Śiva-brahmin family, who has studied the Śiva-āgamas,
wearing a turban and an upper garment, and possessing the auspicious marks on all his limbs."
Having meditated and drawn up water, one should sprinkle it with both hands and with a water-pot (*karaka*).
Regarding that very point, in the *Śatābhiṣeka-paṭala*:
"Whether a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, a Śūdra, or even myself, [or] one born in the natural order (*anuloma*)."
O twice-born ones, [one should worship] a king born from a distinguished lineage,
or a queen, or a feudatory, or a minister, or a domestic priest; or, O Śiva, O son of a Brahmin, a woman born from that same respective caste.
Adorned with the fivefold ornaments, one should perform the consecration (*abhiṣeka*).
On that very point [it is said]: p. 1241) *tatraiva*—
Having stood and completed the twilight prayers (*sandhyā*), the most excellent teacher, having performed his daily rites,
wearing a turban and an upper garment produced from the five types of cow-products,
adorned with the five ornaments of the limbs, and with a mind delighted by the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), [remained there].

In that very [text], in the chapter on occasional worship (naimittikapūjā): "The great substance offered during the sacrifice, such as gold, garments, and so forth, should be given to the preceptor alone, who abides within the five spheres of perception."
In the Svāyambhuva [Purāṇa]:
"One born into a family of Śiva’s twice-born brahmins, who knows the procedure for the yoga-worship, having performed the worship of Naṭeśa specifically according to the rules..."
In the *Suprabheda*:
"The Ācārya, being an initiate of the Śaiva path, having consecrated his body (*sakalīkṛtavigraha*), and having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited,
should sprinkle [the site] with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*)."
One should plough the earth, beginning from the east and moving toward the north, with the *praṇava* and the *Śiva-mantra*.
As stated in the *Kāmika*: "O twice-born ones, for whichever king the exposition of the knowledge of Śiva takes place..."
That kingdom, along with its powerful sovereign, flourishes constantly;
whether in the capacity of a king of kings, as a commander-in-chief, in other duties, as a domestic priest,
or in overseeing all royal affairs.
If he is a Lord of the lineage (*sāntānikeśvara*), he shall be a fit candidate for pure Śaivism.
In that very [text] it is said:
"In the age of Anantakāla, Kauśika and others were initiated there by Śiva."
The twice-born who are born into that lineage are indeed those who subsist on gleanings;
they are to be known as *sāntānika*s, for they desire the acceptance of all [offerings].

Whether they are considered to be engaged in the conduct of [Śaiva] practice (*caraṇācaryā*) or devoid of it, according to the *Vīra-tantra*—in the section on Śiva’s twice-born followers (*śivadvija*)—it is stated:
"O best of Brahmins, the Śiva-dvijas are known as the Ādiśaivas. (Kauśika)
Kāśyapa, Bhāradvāja, Anila,
and Gautama— these five were initiated into the five faces. O best of Brahmins, these sages were born again and again.
One should never perform initiation for Śiva-dvijas;
however, initiation is desired for them for the purpose of my worship and for the purification of their initiation. (From the Kāmika):

The arrangement of the various components of the festival, the offering of gifts to the deities, and so forth; at that time, the procession to the primary *mūla-liṅga* and other sites, and the daily fire-oblation (*nityahoma*)—how can one person perform all these tasks that require many men? Oh, this is well-asked!

O one of great wisdom, I shall explain meditative absorption (*samādhi*). Whatever action—whether obligatory, occasional, or optional—is established in a state of single-minded focus, that should be performed as a solitary practice; this has been well spoken by me.
The son or grandson of this preceptor, or his kinsman;
those men who, though not initiated by him, are filled with fear and reverence for his instructions;
and those born in the lineage of the original Śaiva—whether Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, or Śūdras.
Those who are favorable to me, such as the Gandharvas, dancers, and others,
as well as the daughters of Śūdras who are my servants and observers of my commands—
if they also perform the ritual, it shall be considered as performed by the Preceptor himself.
p. 1243) In the *Sūkṣma* [Tantra],
the installation (*pratiṣṭhā*), consecration (*sthāpanā*), and so forth, should be performed according to the *Ādiśaiva* [tradition].

All those beginning with the *anuśaiva* [and others], in relation to the purpose of the Self, are respectively the *samayin*, the *putraka*, the *sāyaka*, and the *mūrtidhāraka*. If one has gone to another country, one may perform [the rites] by virtue of the Guru’s command.
If the master (*ācārya*) who is born of yoga should pass away while his ritual duties are still extensive, that task must be performed by his son or disciple with his authorization.
In the case of a cause—
when there is a contradiction regarding the very instrument used by the teacher— it is that action which must be performed by the disciple toward him, according to the scripture.
In the *Kāmika*:

"That [worship] is declared for a Brāhmaṇa who has taken refuge in Śiva according to the Śiva-āgama; however, for the three castes beginning with the Kṣatriya, worship for the sake of others is not permitted."
In the Kāmika:
"Therefore, for the sake of others and for one's own sake, as well as for one's own sake, the bathing [rite] should be performed by a Śiva-brahmin;
for others, it is indeed only for their own benefit."
If one should act for the sake of another even by cutting off a limb of the king, then the destruction of that observer will occur before long; of this there is no doubt. As stated in the Vīratantra:
One born in the Ādiśaiva lineage is indeed called a *deśika* (preceptor). By an Ādiśaiva, all rites from the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) to the final worship (*arcanā*) must be performed.
For if one should cause them to be done otherwise, it would surely lead to malevolent magic (*abhicāra*).
In that very same [text]:
"Those Śiva-dvijas who are born into the lineages of those sages do not undergo initiation again; their performance of duties is fruitless."
Regarding the cause—one should perform the festival afterwards for a period of up to seven days.

The best of preceptors (deśikottama) should also cause a festival to be held for one day; from the beginning until the end, it shall be conducted by a single preceptor. In the absence of the preceptor, however, he should have it performed by a mūrtipa, including all the ritual implements for the sacrifice.
One should cause it to be given to the preceptor.
Elsewhere it is said:
"One who has arisen as an Ādiśaiva, and has been consecrated by the initiation of Śiva..."
One who has emerged from the five spheres of sensory experience and is devoted to the practice of Śaivism—
having approached such a guru, one should perform the installation and other rites.
Such individuals are declared to be the guardians of the images (mūrtipās), and they should be brought to the rite of fire-oblation (homakarma).
In the *Kāmika*: "According to the sequence [prescribed] by the Śaiva scriptures and the Siddhānta treatises,
as well as by other systems, the liṅga that is to be installed is of a dual nature."

O assembly of kings, those who are worthy of worship for the prosperity of the sacrificer— whether in their own domain or elsewhere— should be Śaivas and possess authority over all matters. All those excellent twice-born householders who act as Śaivas among all [others] are to be honored.

In the Yāmala, Mantra-tantra, Kāpāla, Pāñcarātraka, Bauddha, Vācārhata, Lāguḍa, and even in the Vaidika systems, as well as in other paths according to the methods prescribed in their respective scriptures—
The Śaivas perform initiation and other rites, as well as the installation of that Liṅga and so forth;
thus, these Śiva-brāhmaṇas who maintain their lineage are worthy of worship by Brāhmaṇas of all castes, and even by renunciants (saṃnyāsins) who are honored by all stages of life (āśramas).
This is because it is heard in the Śiva Āgamas and Purāṇas.
As it is stated in the *Makuṭottara*:

Those who act as if they have perfected their intellects are superior to those [who merely renounce]; among renunciants (saṃnyāsins), the worshippers of Śaṅkara are most excellent. It has been declared that even among great renunciants, the worshipper of Śaṅkara is the most distinguished.

It should be understood from certain other Purāṇas and similar sources that while those born of the lineages of the five sages (*pañcarṣi-gotra*) are *sāntānika* (belonging to a specific lineage) and distinguished, those who are distinct from them are ordinary Brahmins (*sāmānya-vipra*), whereas the *śivadvijas* arise as a mixed caste (*saṃkara*). Thus, this concludes the discussion on the majesty of the *śivadvijas*.

In this context, prohibitions regarding worship performed for the sake of others (*parārtha-pūjā*) have been demonstrated for those other than Śiva-initiated twice-born (*śivadvija*)— namely, for Mahāśaiva Brāhmaṇas and others who are initiated, as well as for uninitiated Brāhmaṇas. Nevertheless, in certain instances...

In the *Suprabheda*, the *Ajita*, the *Āgama*, and other such texts, the worship for the sake of others (*parārthapūjā*) is prescribed for those great Śaivas who have been initiated by Śiva and whose rites have been somehow drawn forth by the excellence of their devotion.
As it is stated in the *Suprabheda*:
"Because they have been brought [to this state] by initiation (dīkṣā), they are therefore called 'Anuśaiva' (subsequent Śaivas).
Having begun thus, [it continues]: "One should especially worship [the deity], whether for one's own sake or for the sake of others."
O Ajita, it is declared in the Śiva-āgama that for a Brāhmaṇa who has taken refuge in Śiva, worship for the sake of others is not permitted for the three castes beginning with the Kṣatriya.
In the *Hālāsya-māhātmya*:
"Brahmins who are devoid of initiation are unworthy of worshipping that Great Liṅga;
likewise, even Kṣatriyas must be initiated."
They all had [the rites] performed by various other brāhmaṇas;
elsewhere—

"Furthermore, having attained the Śaiva [initiation], those twice-born worshippers undergo initiation once again therein; they are indeed worthy to perform worship for their own sake and for the sake of others.
From this, the discernment here is that worship is twofold: Vedic and Śaiva.

In this regard, although the Śaiva worship for the sake of others (*parārthapūjā*) mentioned in the Vedic tradition is said— according to the stated method— to concern those seeking liberation through the initiation of maturation (*paripākadīkṣā*), nevertheless, the Vedic worship for the sake of others belongs exclusively to the great sages and great Śaivas who have been initiated by Śiva as part of their ritual worship (*arcanāṅga*).
It should be performed solely by those belonging to the Vedic tradition according to the method prescribed in the Bodhāyana Sūtra;

however, for those who are not initiated according to the Śiva-dīkṣā rites taught in the Śiva Āgamas, it may be performed in some manner by those who have received Śiva-dīkṣā according to the methods taught in the Vedic Pāśupata and other traditions.

In every respect, rites beginning with plowing and ending with consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*), festivals, and penances depend upon the Śiva-āgama; therefore, those who have not received initiation lack the qualification for these according to the Śiva-āgama. Furthermore, this dependence on it exists even in the supplementary support (*upabṛṃhaṇa*) of the Veda.
It is stated in the Sūta-saṃhitā and other Purāṇas:
"O Brahmins, having taken up with faith and a concentrated mind the Śiva-liṅga, which is characterized by the definitions prescribed in the scripture of the Āgamas."
In the *Brahmottara-khaṇḍa*: "The wise man should consecrate the seat (*pīṭha*) according to the procedure taught in the *Āgamas*.
And in the *Smṛti*:
Even some knowers of the Vedas attain perfection by worshipping the gods through the Tantric path,
and from that they obtain their desired fruit;
likewise, in the Vedic *Parārthamīmāṃsā*, there is the glorious "Lifting Out of Distress."
1247) Even by those who have been initiated, it has been established that [the path] is dependent upon the Śiva-āgama and Śiva-initiation (śivadīkṣā),
as it proceeds in its entirety through those who are qualified for the most excellent and primary rites.

One who prioritizes truth should not perform such an action; indeed, an action performed in that manner is said to produce all faults. Furthermore, according to the Mīmāṃsā and Nyāya systems, among the various forms of worship, the Śiva-tantric worship is supreme; therein, for those who possess the primary qualification, Śiva is the principal object of worship.

In the absence of Brāhmaṇas, the king should somehow cause a Vedic Śiva-pūjā to be performed by one learned in the Vedas. The Paurāṇika method for the supreme Vedic worship is now being set forth. Due to the defects of the Kali age, great delusion will arise among mortals.

Pure devotion to the path of the Vedas will not exist in any way; they will constantly place their faith in paths outside the Vedas. They will become short-lived and especially impoverished, afflicted by mental anguish and physical disease.
They will be tormented by weapons and the like, as well as by tigers, thieves, and so forth; likewise, they will be afflicted by spirits, ghosts, and the like.
Having abandoned the conduct of their caste and stage of life (varṇāśrama), they will especially be devoid of the eightfold [virtues] and other distinctions.
They will repeatedly become helpless across all wombs; therefore, O King, increase the kingdom by installing Sāmba— who possesses the characteristics of liberation—
on the riverbank using the *praṇava* alone.

By offering divine perfumes, flowers, and other such items, one will certainly become a sovereign ruler of the entire earth. One should construct a wonderful temple provided with walls and gate-towers (gopuras),
and offer pure rice along with dancing, singing, and other such delights.
Having established Ṣaṇmukha in the northwest and Vināyaka in the southwest,
one should worship them daily for the prosperity of the king and the kingdom.
The twice-born should perform worship for the prosperity of the king and the kingdom.
By worshipping me there, the king attains victory;
he shall be endowed with long life and health, and he will become liberated. And his enemies—
O King of the Gods, there is no doubt that [the king's enemies] perish;
the kingdom shall be abundant in wealth and grain at all times and in every place. Through my worship, there shall be prosperity everywhere at every season.
"All human beings will be devoted to the conduct prescribed for their respective castes and stages of life; of this there is no doubt, and they shall worship me there.
Thus, even for those Brāhmaṇas other than the Śiva-Brāhmaṇas, [it shall happen] in some way.

Even when spoken of as worship for the sake of others (*parārthapūjā*), it should be understood as being used in a figurative sense (*gauṇavṛtti*). Thus ends the greatness of the Śaiva Ācāryas according to other [traditions]. Now, the procedure for the Śaiva Ācāryas of the four castes (*cāturvarṇya*) is stated.

As it is stated in the Śiva Purāṇa: "Those belonging to the four castes, beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, who are fully endowed with the Śiva-śāstra and are averse to the Paśu-śāstras, are proclaimed as Ācāryas."
In the *Kāmika*:
"In the case of a self-interest sacrifice (*svārtheṣṭi*), there are these three types of installation for a mobile liṅga;
even a Śūdra [is eligible] for a Śūdra-initiation, and for a self-interest [sacrifice], it is designated as 'mobile' (*cala*)."
In the *Suprabheda*:
"Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras born of pure lineages..."
"But they alone are to be known as Ācāryas, and never others"— thus it is stated in that very *Jātinirṇaya*:
"Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras are indeed proclaimed [to be such]."

"One should appoint these members of the four castes to the office of teacher. Thus it is stated in the *Sarvajñānottara*: "Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras are all pure practitioners (*sādhakas*)."

"According to the sequence of one's own caste, and [the sequence] beginning with the teacher and ending with the six-faced one"—thus it should be reflected upon: "In this manner, among the four castes beginning with the Brahmin, and likewise among the six [castes] following the natural order (anuloma) and so forth; for these..."

It is prescribed that the status of teacher (*ācāryatva*) belongs to ten classes. As stated in the *Parākhyatantra*: "From this point on, a Brahmin is the teacher of all castes; a Kṣatriya is the teacher of three [castes]; a Vaiśya and a Śūdra..."
One who understands the purpose of vision and action should unify the two;
the Brāhmaṇa is traditionally held to be the perpetual benefactor of all castes. Among his own caste, there are three types of teachers, while the others—beginning with the Kṣatriya—are subordinate.
Likewise, in the *Ṣaṭsāhasrikā*:
"The status of being a teacher for all four castes is declared here;
and among all castes, the twice-born is considered the benefactor."
A Kṣatriya [is purified] by three [initiations], a Vaiśya by two, and a Śūdra by one born of his own caste.
Thus, the work of bestowing grace is performed by all four types of teachers.
In the *Kiraṇa*, Garuḍa asks: "Tell me, which among the four syllables in the middle possesses weight (*gurutva*)? Īśvara replies:
The status of being a teacher for all four castes is declared here; among the group of four beginning with the Brāhmaṇa, the twice-born is considered the benefactor:
the Kṣatriya for three, the Vaiśya for two, and the Śūdra for his own kind.
Furthermore, in the Kāmika [Tantra]:

"The triad beginning with the daily rites (nitya) should be performed by the four [castes] according to their conduct; likewise, the Śūdra should perform the Vaiśvadeva and the twilight worship (saṃdhyā), excluding that which consists of the Self."
In the *Kālottara*: "Indeed,
one who has been thus consecrated— whether he be a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya,
or even a Śūdra— is unalterable in performing installations and other such rites."

But is it not the case that, because the fourth [chapter] demonstrates the heaviness of the subject matter through various citations, this must pertain to a lifelong celibate (naiṣṭhika) Śūdra and not to a householder?
This has been stated in the Kāmika:
"Even a Śūdra, in the case of a Śūdra-initiation, for his own purpose, or in that which is designated as 'unstable' (cala),
or even upon seeing a Bāṇaliṅga, may become a lifelong consecrator (sthāpaka) and so forth."
"Even for a Śūdra householder, fitness exists only for the *nityeṣṭi* sacrifice;
he is unfit even for the consecration (*abhiṣeka*), so how much more so for the installation (*sthāpana*) and other rites?"—
True, this statement is irrelevant, as it depends solely on the intention of the listener.

Otherwise, according to the maxim "let there be more," it would be entirely meaningless. And so say those who know the nature of sentences: "When there is a conflict and no equal connection, the majority shall prevail."
Regarding one who shares the same nature [as worldly people], the Purāṇa states:
"For the sake of the family, one should abandon an individual; for the sake of the village, one should abandon the family;
for the sake of the country, one should abandon the village; and for the sake of the self, one should abandon the entire earth," and so forth.
Regarding the avoidance of contradiction, this principle was also stated by the venerable Skandara:
"That which is contradicted by the Vedic tradition should be set aside; that which is consistent with the noble [tradition] should be adopted.
A small [matter] should be set aside for the sake of the many, and likewise, one should act separately according to the conduct of the virtuous."
"And there is nothing else. The status of the householder Śūdras as gurus is already established;

furthermore, statements regarding the inferiority of the *naiṣṭhika* (lifelong celibate), such as "the *naiṣṭhika* should be known as lower," must be reconciled by the logic already stated. As it is said in the *Parākhyatantra*:

"In the *Kālottara*, it is stated: 'Among all castes, the householder is declared to be the superior guru; the lifelong celibate (*naiṣṭhika*) is to be known as inferior, and the materialist (*bhautika*) especially so.'"
"In this Siddhānta, the status of an Ācārya has been established by Śiva even for those belonging to the four castes, as well as for householders. Thus it is stated in the *Uttarakāmika*:
"Especially the status of teacher for householders of the four castes, or especially the status of teacher for celibate students. Thus it is stated in the *Ṣaṭsahasrikā*.
Listen, O Six-faced One, to the reality of how enjoyment and liberation exist:
the supreme teacher is of two kinds, namely the celibate student (brahmacārī) and the householder (gṛhastha).

Both of these are qualified for initiation (*dīkṣā*) and installation (*pratiṣṭhā*); however, the celibate student (*brahmacārī*) is to be known as the teacher for those whose sole aim is liberation and who are averse to worldly prosperity, while the householder is the teacher for those who possess both [aims].
"But for those other than householders, there is no entitlement to enjoyment;
therefore, a householder should be made the Guru by those seeking both enjoyment and liberation.
Likewise, in the *Santāna*:

"The householder is the superior [stage], while the student (brahmacārin) would be inferior"—thus it is stated in the *Suprabheda*. Also in the *Ta* * * Tantra: "The householder is to be known as the superior, and the materialist student (bhautika-brahmacārin) as well."

One should know that among those who are celibate students (*brahmacārin*), the householder is superior; yet, among householders, the one seeking offspring (*sāntānika*) is the best, and in his absence, the ordinary householder. Among householders, the lifelong student (*naiṣṭhika*) is the teacher (*deśika*). Or, the student who subsists on alms (*bhauddika*) is the teacher of householders.
"In the case of those who have reached the ultimate goal, the view is that [liberation] occurs through enjoyment and liberation in succession.
In the *Kiraṇatantra*: "The householder teacher is declared to be the best of guides, one who belongs to a spiritual lineage (*sāntānika*)."
"One should know either the householder or the celibate student to be supreme;
the householder is the best of teachers for the sake of attaining both worldly enjoyment and liberation," so it is stated in the Kāmika Āgama.

Those who were initiated by Śiva at the time following creation, such as Kauśika and others—those twice-born ones belonging to that lineage shall become Śivas, [and] those who belong to the lineage of progeny (sāntānika). p. 1252) sāntānikaḥ.

The best of gurus is a householder; in his absence, a *bhautika* celibate (*brahmacārī*) or a lifelong celibate (*naiṣṭhika*) may serve as the instructor in the home. Among those who are lifelong celibates, he is considered the most excellent, as he is held to lead to both worldly enjoyment and liberation in due order.
A householder is said to be the guru for the sake of accomplishing both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
In that very [text] it is said:
"O twice-born ones, one should consecrate [the disciple] in the northern direction of the Great City; in the eastern [direction]..."
Kṣatriyas, Brahmins, and Vaiśyas are in the direction of Yama (the south), while Śūdras are in the western quarter; or all may be situated as they stand.
Even one devoid of all auspicious marks is accepted as a Guru if he possesses knowledge.
"A person who discriminates between those of high and low caste would be a sinner.
Thus ends the *Cāturvarṇya-śaiva-māhātmya*.
The Procedure for Renunciation for the Four Castes.
In the *Cintyaviśva*:
"Ascetics are to be known as threefold—the ascetic (*tapasvin*), the learned (*vidvas*), and the knower (*vidvān*); thus they are declared to be of three kinds. Their characteristics are now stated."
"O observer of excellent vows, the conduct of one who is established in austerity and is an ascetic is as follows: he must never study, nor form any resolve, nor listen [to teachings];
he must not gather disciples, nor reveal his knowledge."
He should speak the refined (Sanskrit) language; he should carry neither a staff nor a water-pot.
Having worshipped the *liṅga* and the rosary with mere devotion, he remains alone.
At the foot of a tree or in a forest devoid of people,
one who is filled with fear of men should dwell using only his arms as a vehicle; he should have a seat made of anything whatsoever,
and likewise food and drink.
"Using the hands as a bowl and the stomach as a vessel, living on food obtained by begging—thus described, one becomes an ascetic;
such a practitioner attains renown.
This, O Lord of Rivers, is the mode of life for both the learned man and the ascetic."

Teaching, studying, listening, and reflecting—these four constitute the specific duties of a learned person, and especially so for one who is wise. For a wise person, however, there is a distinction: exposition and reflection are their particular tasks.

One who is endowed with the initiation of a true preceptor and is well-versed in the forest-dweller’s (āraṇyaka) scriptures is [fit for this]. Threefold [discipline] is prescribed for ascetics (yatīs), and fourfold for the Śaivas within the stages of life (āśramas).
While there is a distinction among those including the Śūdras, no distinction exists in their ultimate steadfastness (*niṣṭhā*). [Thus ends] the two verses.

The fruit is enjoyed, and liberation is common to both. In the *Sūtasaṃhitā*, the *Kiraṇa*, and other texts, these [actions]—such as digging, burning, and cutting—are to be understood through various modes of expression. In the *Suprabheda*:

The four castes, beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, who originated from Kāśyapa and the others, were appointed to their respective offices by the grace of the Supreme Lord. I shall now briefly describe the *gocara* and the *gotrasūtra*. The *gocara*...

The Śiva-symbol is indeed the lineage (*gotra*), and the group of sages; the Sūtra and likewise the Ācāra are thus declared in sequence for the followers of Śiva (*śaiva*). The crest-lock (*śikhā*) is likewise... [p. 1255]
Jyotis, Sāvitrī, and Gocara—these are the four names of the Śaivas in the teaching of Śiva. Gocara is that which is...
and its emblem is of four kinds.
Kāśyapa, Kauśika, Bharadvāja, and Gautama—these four types are to be known as proclaimed here by the Sage.
Indeed, the vow is said to be of two kinds: general and specific. [The student] is a *brahmacārī*.
The householder, the forest-dweller, and the mendicant—
thus indeed is the fourfold stage of life (caturāśrama) prescribed by the general rule; for this Śiva-āgama is equal regarding the spheres of activity of all four.
And in the Kālottara:
"Śiva, Śikhā, Jyotis, and Sāvitrī—this is the tetrad. The Śaiva family is born from Śiva;
the Śikhā family is born from Śakti."

From the Bindu arises the Jyotis-kula, and from the Nāda, the Savitra-kula. When a mantra is dissolved into Śiva and the other [deities] during initiation for a specific desire (kāmya-dīkṣā), the fourfold Kula is produced in succession according to those respective gateways. This is the Krama.
The fourfold group beginning with the Brāhmaṇa is to be known [in this context].
At the dawning of the pure [Kṛta age], that which is natural and established by birth perishes.
In the Kṛta Yuga, a Brāhmaṇa is the best renunciant; in the Tretā Yuga, a Kṣatriya is the renunciant.
In the Dvāpara age, the Vaiśya renunciant is indeed the best; in the Kali age, the Śūdra renunciant is the best. (p. 1856)
The passage beginning with "the most excellent" (*śreṣṭha*) and so forth is to be seen as existing in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa* and other such texts.
Now, [it may be asked]: in the *Sarvajñānottara*—
In the Śaiva tradition, there are two types of practitioners belonging to the stages of life (āśramins): the householder and the student;
they are the ones who perform grace for the world, whereas the wandering mendicant (parivrāj) and the ascetic (tāpasa) are not.
As stated in the Kālottara:
In the *Suprabheda*, it is always maintained that for those who have passed beyond the stage of the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*), the state of the guru is desired;
for when these renunciants (*saṃnyāsīnaḥ*) abandon the fire of the elements and substances, [the initiation] occurs.

If it is asked: "Since there are prohibitive statements such as 'Therefore, they [the Sannyāsins] are not at all qualified for installation (sthāpanā),' how can you say that Sannyāsins possess the nature of a *mṛga*?"—it is true; however, apart from the *āṇavī* initiation (*dīkṣā*) consisting of powers like *aṇimā*, there are two types of initiation: the *śāktī* and the *śāmbhavī*.
In that initiation characterized by knowledge (*jñānavatī-dīkṣā*), there certainly exists a certain degree of guru-hood in some cases.

As it is stated in the *Sannyāsadīpikā* regarding the two types of renunciants—the *parahaṃsa-yatis* and the *tapas-sannyāsins*: "The eligibility for fire-rituals (*agnikārya*) is not prescribed for these two."

Thus, the consecration for these two is prescribed even without the *homa* offering; this concludes the ritual procedure for Śaiva renunciation (*śaivasannyāsa*). [Now follows] the ritual procedure for the worship of Śiva (*śivapūjāvidhi*).
In the Raurava hell, the [image] of a Brahmin should be white in color; for a Kṣatriya, it should be red; for a Vaiśya, it should be yellow;
and for a Śūdra, it should be black.
Regarding the essence:
white, red, yellow, and black— these four colors correspond respectively to the four castes,
beginning with the Brahmins (bhūsuras) and ending with the Śūdras.
Alternatively, that [mantra] which is black in color may be worthy of all castes.
As stated in the *Kālottara*:
Due to its absence [of other colors], the black color bestows success among all castes.
In that very same [text]:
"The black [color] bestows the accomplishment of all aims and is beneficial for the four castes."
Alternatively, if it is desired that the Bāṇaliṅga grant liberation to all, [it should be made as follows]:
for a Brāhmaṇa, it should be subtle; for a Kṣatriya, it should be octagonal (vasra-aśra); for a Vaiśya, [it should be hexagonal].
The square [seat] belongs to the Śūdra, while the circular one belongs to the [other castes];
the wise man should fashion a circular seat for all castes.
Thus it is stated in the Vidyāsārasaṃhitā:
A *rasaliṅga* shall grant all desired objects to Brāhmaṇas;
a red *liṅga* (*raktaliṅga*) shall grant great sovereignty to Kṣatriyas;
a golden *liṅga* (*svarṇaliṅga*) shall grant the status of a great lord of wealth to Vaiśyas; and a stone *liṅga* (*śilāliṅga*)...
They know that the crystal Bāṇaliṅga bestows great sovereignty upon Śūdras and grants all desires to everyone. For women, especially those with husbands, the earthen liṅga is prescribed.

O observers of excellent vows, for widows who have desisted from worldly life, there is a sequence beginning with the *rasaliṅga* and others, whether in childhood, youth, or old age; indeed, for women,
a *śuddhasphaṭika-liṅga* (liṅga of pure crystal) leads to immediate liberation.
Aṃśumatī said:
"Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and even Śūdras who have been initiated may perform worship for their own sake, but they should not perform it for the sake of others."
p.
1258) And specifically, the worship of women born of the four castes [is prescribed];
thus ends the procedure for the one who performs the rite of Śiva-pūjā.
A statement containing faults that leads to the commission of the fault of reviling Śiva and others is as follows.
In the *Jñānapāda* of the *Suprabhedāgama*:
"One who misappropriates the property of the deity, one who reviles the scriptures of Śiva, and one who harms his father..."
Killers of Brahmins and others such as these fall into the ocean of hell, taking refuge in various places of torment;
as stated in the *Upadeśakāṇḍa*:
These six elephants likewise revile Śambhu and the others, as well as the auspicious baths,
the Vedas, the sacred ash, rudrākṣa beads, the Āgamas, the Śaiva scriptures,
and other supreme texts related to Śiva.
Indeed, he is declared to be a deluded soul who remains near a reviler,
as well as one who hears, sees, touches, or converses with him.
Listening to such speech is likewise declared to be an offense against Śiva.
In the *Rūpākṣa-māhātmya*, the first part of the essence of all Purāṇas beginning with the *Brahmāṇḍa*:
"The scripture of Śiva, the conduct of Śiva, the mantra of Śiva, the collection of Śiva, and the world of Śiva..."
Those sinful ones who treat with contempt the knowledge of Śiva, meditation on Śiva, worship of Śiva,
the power of Śiva, hymns to Śiva, the sacred sites of Śiva, and the scriptures of Śiva—
may they remain perpetually bound in dense darkness.
Whether it be a Śaiva, a Pāśupata, a Kālāmukha, or one who wears the skull-bowl (Kāpāla)—
if he were to kill the entire world, it would be as good as killed by that evil-minded man.
In the *Skāndapurāṇa*, in the *Śikhaṇḍa* section, these are the words of Śiva addressed to Viṣṇu:
"Furthermore, those other lowest of men who, while residing in my hermitage, revile the four castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, even though they are endowed with the armor and weapons of Śiva."
O best of gods, they will undoubtedly become heretics;

for them, whatever is performed—whether ascetic penance, fire-offerings, chanting, ritual bathing, meditation, or worship—all becomes as fruitless as an oblation poured into ashes. They shall be devoted to my hermitage.
O Mādhava, he who hates me when I am free from hatred,
and he who praises me when I am praising one devoted to my hermitage—
these, as well as Brahmā, Indra, the Sun, and other deities, will act otherwise, O you who are deluded by illusion.
O beloved, whether they be Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, or others, all are capable of protecting those about to fall into the ocean of hell if they possess self-control.
Possessing those same attributes, they were established in the abode of Śiva;
all were said to wear matted hair, their bodies smeared with ashes,
and all eating in a single row, O fair-faced one.
Having received this mantra, one must certainly not utter one's former birth-status, whether for the sake of *putrakas*,
*sādhakas*, or even *samayins*. O God, by uttering one's former birth-status, one becomes subject to a different penance for three days.
He shall be cooked in hell for five days for Rudra, for one [day] for Keśava, and for one fortnight for the Grandfather (Brahmā), O Brāhmaṇas.

The Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras are indeed the Supreme Goddess; in their state of life and in their secret essence, they all abide as Śivā. Those lowest of men who perceive them otherwise than in their primordial nature [are deluded].
They are cooked in hell for three years known as *sāda*.
In the *Kāśī-khaṇḍa*:
"The fool who delights in reviling Śiva and who censures the scriptures of Śiva—for him there is no [liberation]."
Having seen [this] in some scripture for the sake of expiation,
it is also stated in the *Sūta-saṃhitā*:
"If there exists the knowledge of Brahman, whether in a woman or in a man, [regardless of] caste or stage of life..."
"O believers,

for one who does not know the self-knowledge pertaining to their own caste and stage of life (varṇāśrama), there is indeed no proper conduct at all; that deluded soul abandons [dharma]— thus it is stated in the Manusmṛti regarding the tripuṇḍra."
The twice-born and others must always wear ashes.
And in the *Vṛddhācalamāhātmya*:

"In the sacred place, during recitation (*japa*), fire-offerings (*homa*), on auspicious lunar days (*tithi*), during the worship of the deity, initiation (*dīkṣā*), and at the two types of ancestral rites (*śrāddha*)."

If one who has performed [the rites] is made fearful while wearing a rosary of rudrākṣa beads, then the entire lifespan and Vedic ritual action would have its fruit rendered inexhaustible; yet if this [fear] occurs, it becomes useless— alas,
this would be a faultless well!
O Aṃśumatī,
without the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), there is no śrāddha; without the triple mark, there is no oblation (homa).
"Any gift given without the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) is proclaimed to be demonic.
Therefore, it is certain that those men who are intent on practicing the specific disciplines prescribed in the Śiva Āgamas attain abundant spiritual merits.
Thus ends the *Śivāgamādimāhātmyasaṃgraha*, composed by the venerable Jñānaprakāśaguru, a resident of Śālīvāṭipura.
